shape.figures: an Argand diagram, a curve sketch with its asymptotes, a region to be rotated, a 3-D configuration for a vector question, a scatter diagram, a normal curve, a tree diagram, a printed table of data
shape.notation: H2 notation: \mathrm{f}: x \mapsto \ldots, \mathrm{f}^{-1}, \mathrm{fg}, column vectors \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix} (also \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j}, \mathbf{k}), \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{a} + \lambda\mathbf{b}, \mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{n} = d, \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}, z^{*}, \arg z, \sum_{r=1}^{n}, u_n and S_n, \mathrm{N}(\mu, \sigma^2), \mathrm{B}(n, p), \bar{X}, \mathrm{H}_0 and \mathrm{H}_1, \mathrm{P}(A \mid B), \mathrm{e}^{x}.
shape.scope: PURE MATHEMATICS (all of Paper 1; Section A of Paper 2). Functions: domain and range, one-one functions and inverses (restricting a domain so that an inverse exists; the graph of f^{-1} as the reflection of f in y = x; the domain of f^{-1} is the range of f), composite functions and the condition for fg to exist, repeated composition (f^2, f^{2025}(x) by finding the pattern); NOT (fg)^{-1} = g^{-1}f^{-1}, NOT restricting a domain to make a composite exist. Graphs and transformations: sketching y = (ax+b)/(cx+d) and y = (ax^2+bx+c)/(dx+e) with their asymptotes (vertical, horizontal, oblique), intercepts, turning points and symmetry; y^2 = ax, x^2 = by, the ellipse x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1 and the hyperbolas x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = 1, y^2/b^2 - x^2/a^2 = 1; the transformations y = af(x), y = f(x) + a, y = f(x + a), y = f(ax) and combinations described as a SEQUENCE (order matters); the graphs of y = |f(x)|, y = f(|x|) and y = 1/f(x) from y = f(x); simple parametric curves and their sketches. Equations and inequalities: formulating an equation, a system of linear equations (solved on the graphing calculator) or an inequality from a situation; solving an equation exactly or numerically; inequalities f(x)/g(x) > 0 with linear or quadratic f and g by a sign test, never by cross-multiplying; the modulus and |x - a| < b <=> a - b < x < a + b, |x - a| > b <=> x < a - b or x > a + b; solving an inequality from a sketch, and a related inequality by a substitution (x -> |x|, x -> e^x) into one already solved. Sequences and series: a sequence as a function of n, the relation u_n = S_n - S_{n-1}, sequences given by a formula or by a recurrence u_{n+1} = f(u_n) (generating terms, a limit L satisfying L = f(L) when the sequence converges, the behaviour read from a graph or a table), sum and difference of two series, convergence of a series and the sum to infinity, arithmetic and geometric series (nth term, sum to n terms, the condition |r| < 1 for convergence, the sum to infinity), finance and other models built on them (savings with increasing deposits, a loan with monthly interest and repayments, a bouncing ball); NOT the method of differences (removed in the revised 9758 — never set a telescoping sum; a sum whose result is GIVEN may be used for a change of variable), NOT mathematical induction. Vectors: 2-D and 3-D vectors, position, displacement and direction vectors, magnitude, unit vectors, distance between points, collinearity, the ratio theorem (a point dividing a line in a given ratio, midpoints), the scalar product (angle between vectors, a . n-hat as a length of projection, perpendicularity), the vector product (area of a triangle or parallelogram, |a x n-hat| as a perpendicular distance, a normal to a plane); vector and cartesian equations of lines and of planes (r . n = d, r = a + lambda b + mu c, cartesian); the foot of the perpendicular from a point to a line or a plane and the distance, the reflection of a point in a line or a plane; the angle between two lines, a line and a plane, two planes; the relationship between two lines (intersecting, parallel, skew), a line and a plane (meets in a point, lies in it, parallel to it), two planes (the line of intersection); problems in a stated 3-D situation (an aircraft path, a pipeline under a plane of rock); NOT the shortest distance or common perpendicular between two skew lines, NOT triple products. Complex numbers: extending the number system, complex roots of a quadratic, conjugate roots of a polynomial equation with real coefficients (and using them to find unknown real coefficients or the remaining root), modulus, argument (principal, in (-pi, pi]) and conjugate, the four operations in cartesian form, equality of complex numbers (a pair of simultaneous equations in z and w solved by elimination or by comparing real and imaginary parts), the Argand diagram, the geometrical effect of conjugation, negation, addition, subtraction and multiplication by i (a rotation through a right angle); NOT polar or modulus-argument form, NOT exponential form r e^{i theta}, NOT de Moivre, NOT loci. Differentiation: the sign of f' and f'' read from and drawn on a graph, the graph of y = f'(x) from y = f(x), implicit and parametric differentiation, the nature of stationary points by the first or second derivative test, tangents and normals (including to implicit and parametric curves, and where a tangent meets the curve again or passes through a given point), maxima and minima in a modelled situation (an area, a volume, a cost) with the maximum shown to be one, connected rates of change (a bowl filling, a ladder, a shadow); NOT non-stationary points of inflexion, NOT the second derivative of a parametric curve. Maclaurin series: the standard series for (1+x)^n with rational n, e^x, sin x, cos x, ln(1+x) with their ranges of validity (all in MF26), the first terms of a series by repeated differentiation (also from a differential relation such as dy/dx = k e^x (1 + y^2), differentiating that relation again), by repeated implicit differentiation, or by multiplying and substituting standard series (e^x cos 2x, ln((1+x)/(1-x)), (1+x)^n with a non-integer n, tan^{-1}(sqrt 2 + x) via its derivatives), the series as an approximation (an integral estimated from its first terms, a value of pi or ln 2), small-angle approximations sin x ~ x, cos x ~ 1 - x^2/2, tan x ~ x; NOT the general term. Integration techniques: f'(x)[f(x)]^n (n = -1 included), f'(x) e^{f(x)}, sin^2 x, cos^2 x, tan^2 x and products of sines and cosines via the factor formulae, the four standard forms 1/(x^2 + a^2), 1/sqrt(a^2 - x^2), 1/(x^2 - a^2), 1/(a^2 - x^2) (results in MF26), partial fractions, integration by a GIVEN substitution (including a trigonometric one for sqrt(a^2 - x^2)), integration by parts (including ln x, x^2 e^x, e^x sin x by two rounds), a modulus integrand split at its zero; NOT reduction formulae. Definite integrals: the integral as a limit of a sum, area under and between curves and lines (regions below the x-axis, areas against the y-axis, a parametric curve via integral y (dx/dt) dt), volumes of revolution about the x-axis or the y-axis (a cartesian curve, a region between two curves, a spherical cap or a bowl), exact values by hand where asked and numerical values from the graphing calculator otherwise; NOT the volume of revolution of a parametric curve. Differential equations: general and particular solutions of dy/dx = f(x) g(y) by separating variables, including reducing an equation to that form by a GIVEN substitution, second-order equations of the form d^2y/dx^2 = f(x) or a first-order equation in v = dx/dt by direct integration, formulating an equation from a situation (rate of change proportional to the amount, rate in minus rate out, a logistic-type dP/dt = kP(N - P), Newton cooling, a falling parachutist), interpreting the solution and its long-term behaviour, sketching the solution curve. PROBABILITY AND STATISTICS (Section B of Paper 2 only). Probability and counting: the addition and multiplication principles, permutations and combinations, arrangements in a line or a circle with repetition and restrictions (identical objects, objects together, objects separated), selection of committees with conditions; addition and multiplication of probabilities, mutually exclusive and independent events (tested numerically), tables of outcomes, Venn diagrams, tree diagrams and counting methods for probabilities, conditional probability P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B), P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B), games with turns and geometric-series probabilities, probabilities in terms of an unknown n or p. Discrete random variables: a probability distribution from a table, expectation and variance from it, E(aX + b) and Var(aX + b); the binomial distribution B(n, p) as a model with its two conditions stated in context (independent trials, a constant probability), its mean np and variance np(1 - p), probabilities and cumulative probabilities from the graphing calculator, the most likely value, a binomial on top of a binomial (the number of days on which an event happens), the range of p from a modal value; NOT cumulative distribution functions, NOT the Poisson distribution (removed from 9758), NOT the geometric distribution, NOT the normal approximation to the binomial. Normal distribution: N(mu, sigma^2) as a model, the standard normal, probabilities and inverse probabilities from the graphing calculator, the symmetry of the curve (drawn with its main features), finding mu and/or sigma from one or two given probabilities (standardising and solving), E and Var of aX + b and of aX + bY with X and Y independent (the sum of n independent copies X_1 + ... + X_n against the multiple nX; the difference of two totals; a percentage reduction as a scaling), the mass exceeded by a given percentage; NOT the normal approximation to the binomial. Sampling: population and simple random sample, why and how a random sample is taken and what makes one unsuitable, the sample mean as a random variable with E(X-bar) = mu and Var(X-bar) = sigma^2/n, its distribution from a normal population, the Central Limit Theorem for a large sample from any population (n >= 30 as the rule of thumb), unbiased estimates of the population mean and variance from raw data or from summarised data (sum x and sum x^2, or sum (x - a) and sum (x - a)^2). Hypothesis testing: null and alternative hypotheses stated with the parameter defined, the test statistic, critical region and critical value, level of significance and p-value, a test of a population mean from a normal population with known variance or from a large sample (a z-test), one-tail and two-tail tests and the reason for the choice, the conclusion in the context of the question, the assumptions a test needs, the range of a significance level or of a variance consistent with a stated conclusion; NOT the terms Type I and Type II error, NOT a test of the difference of two means, NOT a t-test. Correlation and linear regression: a scatter diagram and what it shows, the product moment correlation coefficient as a measure of linear fit and its interpretation (values near -1, 0 and 1; unaffected by a change of units), the least-squares regression line (the meaning of the residuals and of least squares; y on x, and x on y, and which to use), interpolation and extrapolation and the reliability of an estimate, a square, reciprocal, logarithmic or other transformation to achieve linearity and the choice between candidate models by comparing r; NOT deriving the formulae, NOT r^2 = b_1 b_2, NOT hypothesis tests on r. ASSUMED KNOWLEDGE (O-Level A Math): quadratics and the discriminant, surds, polynomials and partial fractions, binomial theorem for a positive integer index, indices and logarithms, trigonometric identities and the R-formula, the sine and cosine rules, basic differentiation and integration.
shape.register:
REGISTER — how SEAB asks (9758)
- Plain, exact, economical English. Every part is an imperative: Find, Show that, Hence (or Hence, or otherwise), Deduce, State, Sketch, Explain (why / whether / how you know / in context), Determine (whether / the possible values), Verify, Use … to …, Write down, Solve, Express, Describe (a sequence of transformations; the set of points; the relationship), Justify your answer, Give a reason, Suggest.
- Parts are (a), (b), (c) with sub-parts (i), (ii); every leaf part carries its marks in [ ]; a 3–6 mark question may be unparted. The parts of a long question BUILD: an early "Show that" prints the result the later parts need, and "Hence", "Using the result in part (b)" or "Use your answer to part (c)(i)" says so.
- Precision is stated when it matters: "giving your answer in exact form", "in the form a + ib where a and b are real numbers", "correct to 3 significant figures", "in terms of p", "to the nearest cent", "correct to 2 decimal places", "as a single simplified fraction"; otherwise the rubric's 3 s.f. applies and nothing is said. "Find exactly", "Find the exact value" and "Solve exactly" forbid a decimal; "Use calculus", "Using calculus", "By integration" and "Show by integration" forbid a calculator read-off; "Do not use a calculator in answering this question." opens a whole question (a complex-number question, an exact-integral question, an exact inequality); "Without using a calculator" opens a part. Section B says "State the distribution you use", "In this question you should state the parameters of any distributions you use", "Define any symbols you use", "Give your conclusion in the context of the question".
- The graphing calculator is assumed. Numerical roots, definite integrals, the regression constants, r, binomial and normal probabilities and inverse-normal values are READ from it and the question asks only for the value — a question that wants the working says so. Where a graph is used to find a solution the candidate sketches it. Unsupported calculator answers earn no method marks, so a 4-mark part is never a single calculator read.
- Notation is the syllabus's: \mathrm{f}: x \mapsto \frac{ax+k}{x-a}, x \in \mathbb{R}, x \neq a; \mathrm{f}(x), \mathrm{f}^{-1}, \mathrm{fg}, \mathrm{f}^2; \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}, \frac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2}, \int \ldots \,\mathrm{d}x; \sum_{r=1}^{n}; u_n and S_n; column vectors and \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j}, \mathbf{k}; \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{a} + \lambda\mathbf{b}; \mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{n} = d; the cartesian line \frac{x+2}{3} = \frac{y-1}{2} = z - 5; z^{*}, |z|, \arg z; \mathrm{N}(\mu, \sigma^2), \mathrm{B}(n, p), \bar{X}, \mathrm{H}_0: \mu = 17.3, \mathrm{P}(A \mid B). Angles in radians unless degrees are named; \mathrm{e}^{x}, \ln x, \mathrm{i} upright.
- Contexts are brief, concrete and self-contained; they carry the numbers the model needs and nothing more (a pipeline under a river, an ornament cut from a sphere, a parachutist, a roller-coaster loop, savings then a loan, a company's two machines, a swimmer's times, a bird feeder, a quality-control sample). Units are given; constants are named ("where k is a positive constant", "where \alpha is a constant"). No story, no chattiness, no names beyond one or two.
- Paper 1 opens with 4–6-mark questions (a system of equations, an inequality, a vector fact, a complex-number question, a short sequence question) and climbs to two or three 12–15-mark closers — a differential-equation model, a vector problem in a stated 3-D situation, a finance question on arithmetic and geometric series, a parametric or graph model, a functions question with several parts — with one question that "may require concepts and skills from more than one topic" in a real-world context. Paper 2 Section A is four (occasionally five) pure questions of 6–13 marks; Section B climbs from a 5–6-mark probability or counting starter through binomial, normal, sampling and hypothesis-testing questions to a 12–17-mark closer, usually the regression or the normal-plus-test question, set in a real-world context.
- Section B asks for words as often as numbers: "State, in context, two assumptions needed for X to be well modelled by a binomial distribution", "Explain whether … should use a one-tailed or a two-tailed test", "State hypotheses for the test, defining any parameters you use", "give your conclusion in the context of the question", "Explain whether your estimate is reliable", "Explain what the scatter diagram tells you about the relationship", "Explain whether the 65 members comprise a sample or a population", "Explain why it is reasonable to assume that the two distributions are independent". A 1-mark explain part expects one sentence with the reason in it; a 2-mark one, two distinct points.
- Marks follow the work at about 1.8 minutes a mark (100 marks in 3 hours). 1–2 marks: state / write down / one deduction / one calculator value. 3–4: one standard routine, or a routine with one decision. 5–6: a routine with a decision and a second idea, a model built from the situation, or a proof. 7 or more in ONE part is rare and needs a chain (a differential equation solved from a substitution to a particular solution; a regression model chosen, fitted and used). Marks climb through each paper and through each section.

sections.b: Section B: Probability and Statistics [60 marks]

title: H2 Mathematics · Set 1 · Paper 2 · A-Level format

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Without using a calculator, solve the inequality $|x-4| < \dfrac{3}{x}$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Deduce the set of values of $x$ for which $|x-4| \geqslant \dfrac{3}{x}$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Hence solve exactly the inequality $\left|\ln x - 4\right| \geqslant \dfrac{3}{\ln x}$.

question.answer: (a) $0 < x < 1$ or $3 < x < 2+\sqrt{7}$ (b) $x < 0$ or $1 \leqslant x \leqslant 3$ or $x \geqslant 2+\sqrt{7}$ (c) $0 \leqslant x \leqslant \ln 3$ or $x \geqslant \ln\left(2+\sqrt{7}\right)$
skills: deducing $x > 0$ because a modulus can never be less than a negative quantity, before multiplying through, so that $|x-4| < \frac{3}{x}$ becomes the double quadratic inequality $-3 < x^2-4x < 3$
complement of a solution set on a domain that excludes $x = 0$: every negative $x$ satisfies the reversed non-strict inequality and the critical values join the set

substitution $x \to \mathrm{e}^{x}$ recognised through $\mathrm{e}^{2x}-4\mathrm{e}^{x} = \mathrm{e}^{x}(\mathrm{e}^{x}-4)$ with $\mathrm{e}^{x} > 0$, the negative branch rejected and the rest converted by logarithms
the substitution x → ln x into a solved inequality, every branch converted by exponentials with the domain x > 0 of ln x noted
question.solution:
(a) Since $|x-4| \geqslant 0$ for every $x$, the inequality can hold only if $\frac{3}{x} > 0$, i.e. $x > 0$: for $x < 0$ the right-hand side is negative and no $x$ satisfies it, and $x = 0$ is excluded.   [B1: $x > 0$ with the reason]
For $x > 0$, multiplying by $x$ keeps the direction: $x|x-4| < 3$, and since $x > 0$, $x|x-4| = |x(x-4)| = |x^2-4x|$. So
$|x^2-4x| < 3 \iff -3 < x^2-4x < 3$.   [M1: modulus removed correctly once the sign of $x$ is known]
$x^2-4x > -3 \iff x^2-4x+3 > 0 \iff (x-1)(x-3) > 0 \iff x < 1$ or $x > 3$.
$x^2-4x < 3 \iff x^2-4x-3 < 0$; the roots of $x^2-4x-3 = 0$ are $x = 2 \pm \sqrt{7}$, so $2-\sqrt{7} < x < 2+\sqrt{7}$.   [A1: critical values $1$, $3$ and $2 \pm \sqrt{7}$]
Combining with $x > 0$ (note $2-\sqrt{7} < 0$): $0 < x < 1$ or $3 < x < 2+\sqrt{7}$.   [A1]
(Alternative by cases, after $x > 0$: for $x \geqslant 4$, $x-4 < \frac{3}{x} \iff x^2-4x-3 < 0 \iff 4 \leqslant x < 2+\sqrt{7}$, as $2+\sqrt{7} \approx 4.65$; for $0 < x < 4$, $4-x < \frac{3}{x} \iff x^2-4x+3 > 0 \iff 0 < x < 1$ or $3 < x < 4$. The union is the same set.)
(The error the part is built to catch: multiplying by $x$ without first establishing $x > 0$ gives $x|x-4| < 3$, which every negative $x$ satisfies, so $x < 0$ is wrongly added to the answer. For $x < 0$ the multiplication reverses the inequality, $x|x-4| > 3$, which is impossible since the left side is not positive.)
Check: $x = \frac{1}{2}$: $3.5 < 6$, true; $x = 2$: $2 < 1.5$, false; $x = 4$: $0 < 0.75$, true; $x = 5$: $1 < 0.6$, false.

(b) $|x-4| \geqslant \frac{3}{x}$ holds exactly where the inequality in (a) fails, among real $x \neq 0$ (the right-hand side is undefined at $x = 0$). Every $x < 0$ satisfies it (left side $\geqslant 0 >$ right side), and the critical values $1$, $3$ and $2+\sqrt{7}$, where the two sides are equal, are now included:
$x < 0$ or $1 \leqslant x \leqslant 3$ or $x \geqslant 2+\sqrt{7}$.   [B1]

(c) $\mathrm{e}^{2x}-4\mathrm{e}^{x} = \mathrm{e}^{x}(\mathrm{e}^{x}-4)$ and $\mathrm{e}^{x} > 0$, so $\left|\mathrm{e}^{2x}-4\mathrm{e}^{x}\right| = \mathrm{e}^{x}\left|\mathrm{e}^{x}-4\right|$ and the inequality becomes $\left|\mathrm{e}^{x}-4\right| \geqslant \frac{3}{\mathrm{e}^{x}}$, which is the inequality in (b) with $x$ replaced by $\mathrm{e}^{x}$.   [M1: the link to (b) through $x \to \mathrm{e}^{x}$]
Hence $\mathrm{e}^{x} < 0$ (rejected, since $\mathrm{e}^{x} > 0$ for all $x$) or $1 \leqslant \mathrm{e}^{x} \leqslant 3$ or $\mathrm{e}^{x} \geqslant 2+\sqrt{7}$,
so $0 \leqslant x \leqslant \ln 3$ or $x \geqslant \ln\left(2+\sqrt{7}\right)$.   [A1]
Check: $x = 0$: $|1-4| = 3$ (equality); $x = \ln 3$: $|9-12| = 3$ (equality); $x = \ln\left(2+\sqrt{7}\right)$: $\mathrm{e}^{2x}-4\mathrm{e}^{x} = \left(2+\sqrt{7}\right)\left(\sqrt{7}-2\right) = 7-4 = 3$ (equality); $x = -1$: $|0.135-1.472| = 1.34 < 3$, so excluded; $x = 1.3$: $|13.46-14.68| = 1.21 < 3$, so excluded.
(Otherwise: with $u = \mathrm{e}^{x} > 0$, $|u^2-4u| \geqslant 3 \iff u^2-4u \geqslant 3$ or $u^2-4u \leqslant -3$, giving $u \geqslant 2+\sqrt{7}$ ($u \leqslant 2-\sqrt{7}$ rejected as $u > 0$) or $1 \leqslant u \leqslant 3$: the same answer.)

(c) [revised at moderation] Put u = ln x (x > 0). The inequality is |u − 4| ≥ 3/u, so by (b): u < 0, or 1 ≤ u ≤ 3, or u ≥ 2 + √7. Hence 0 < x < 1, or e ≤ x ≤ e^3, or x ≥ e^{2+√7}. M1 for the substitution with all three branches carried, A1 for the three sets with the strict 0 < x < 1 (u < 0 means 0 < x < 1; u = 0 is excluded since 3/u is undefined).
question.syllabus_check: 9758 Equations and inequalities: an inequality with a variable denominator solved without cross-multiplying blindly (the sign of $x$ settled first), the modulus removed via $|x-a| < b \iff a-b < x < a+b$ or by cases, quadratic inequalities (assumed knowledge), the complementary non-strict inequality on a domain with $x \neq 0$, and a related inequality solved by the substitution $x \to \mathrm{e}^{x}$ into one already solved. 'Without using a calculator' sits on part (a) only, not on the whole question (Paper 1 Q4 owns the whole-question ban); (c) says 'solve exactly', so no decimal is accepted. The substitution is $x \to \mathrm{e}^{x}$, not $x \to |x|$ (Paper 1 Q6 used $\mathrm{f}(|x|)$). No figure; exact answers throughout ($2+\sqrt{7}$, $\ln 3$, $\ln(2+\sqrt{7})$).
question.originality_note: No earlier Set has an inequality question, and nothing in this paper yet. Not a re-skin of a real paper: GCE 2023 P2 Q1 is a modulus-versus-modulus inequality then a rational inequality combined into one fraction; GCE 2024 P1 Q4 is a rational sign test followed by the $x \to |x|$ substitution; GCE 2025 P1 Q5 is a quadratic in $\mathrm{e}^{x}$ followed by an integral of a modulus; GCE 2019 P1 Q4 and GCE 2019 P2 Q2 are sketch-then-read questions. Here the modulus is bounded by a reciprocal, so the sign of $x$ must be settled before anything is multiplied (the trap that adds every negative $x$), (b) takes the complement on a domain with a hole at $0$, where the negative reals come back in and the critical values join, and (c) must be recognised as (b) under $x \to \mathrm{e}^{x}$ through the factor $\mathrm{e}^{x}(\mathrm{e}^{x}-4)$, with the negative branch lost to $\mathrm{e}^{x} > 0$.

answers.(c): 0 < x < 1 or e \leqslant x \leqslant e^{3} or x \geqslant e^{2+\sqrt{7}}

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both give 0 < x < 1 or 3 < x < 2 + \sqrt{7}. Checked: |x-4| >= 0 forces 3/x > 0 so x > 0; then |x^2 - 4x| < 3 gives (x-1)(x-3) > 0 and 2 - \sqrt{7} < x < 2 + \sqrt{7}; intersected with x > 0 the set is (0, 1) u (3, 2 + \sqrt{7}). Spot checks x = 1/2 (3.5 < 6), x = 2 (2 < 1.5 false), x = 4 (0 < 0.75), x = 4.7 (0.7 < 0.638 false) agree.

parts.label: (b)
parts.note: Both give x < 0 or 1 <= x <= 3 or x >= 2 + \sqrt{7}. The complement on x != 0: every negative x satisfies it (left side >= 0 > right side), and equality holds at 1, 3 and 2 + \sqrt{7} (at the last, both sides equal \sqrt{7} - 2), so the critical values join.

parts.label: (c)
parts.note: Both give 0 <= x <= \ln 3 or x >= \ln(2 + \sqrt{7}). With u = e^x > 0, |u^2 - 4u| = u|u - 4| >= 3 is (b) in u; the branch u < 0 is empty, leaving 1 <= u <= 3 or u >= 2 + \sqrt{7}. Equality at x = 0 (|1 - 4| = 3), x = \ln 3 (|9 - 12| = 3) and x = \ln(2 + \sqrt{7}) ((2 + \sqrt{7})(\sqrt{7} - 2) = 3); x = -1 and x = 1.2 are correctly excluded.

verdict.key_verdict: The setter and the blind examiner agree on every part and both are right; the key is exactly correct.
fixes: This paper tests 'a quadratic in e^x with a root or branch rejected by positivity' twice: here in (c) (u = e^x, the branch u < 0 rejected) and in Q3(a) (the inverse of a function quadratic in e^x, the root chosen by the domain). Since Q3 is the later slot the session may prefer to change Q3; if this slot is to change instead, keep (a) and (b) and replace the map in (c) by one that keeps the negative branch alive so the x < 0 trap of (b) carries real weight, e.g. 'Hence solve exactly |ln x - 4| >= 3/(ln x)' giving 0 < x < 1 or e <= x <= e^3 or x >= e^{2+\sqrt{7}} (the skill becomes: the substitution x -> ln x, all three branches converted by exponentials, with the domain x > 0 of ln x noted).
verdict.why: A clean SEAB-register Section A opener whose two ideas belong to the candidate: in (a) that a modulus cannot be below a negative quantity, so x > 0 must be established before multiplying through (every route, including cases, has to meet the sign of x), and in (c) that e^{2x} - 4e^x = e^x(e^x - 4) with e^x > 0 turns the disguised inequality into (b) under x -> e^x, the intermediate form unprinted; (b)'s non-strict complement with the x < 0 branch is the twist of standard.md item 4. It borrows the 'hence, by substitution' device of GCE 2024 P1 Q4 but with a different inequality type, a complement step and a disguised map, so it is not a re-skin, and no Set 1 P1 question touches inequalities; marks match 2023 P2 Q1(b)/2024 P1 Q4 within a mark and the whole is finishable in about 12 minutes.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Show that $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \frac{x^2 - y^2}{2xy}$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Find the coordinates of any stationary points on $C$, and determine their nature.
parts.answer: $(-2, 2)$, a minimum point ($\frac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2} = \frac{1}{2} > 0$); $(-2, -2)$, a maximum point ($\frac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2} = -\frac{1}{2} < 0$)

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Determine whether there is any point on $C$ at which the tangent to $C$ passes through the origin. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: There is no such point: for the tangent at $(p, q)$ to pass through $O$, $q = p\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$, which (as $q \neq 0$) gives $p^2 = 3q^2$; then $p^3 - 3pq^2 = p(p^2 - 3q^2) = 0 \neq 16$, a contradiction (and the only tangent parallel to the $y$-axis, $x = \sqrt[3]{16}$, does not pass through $O$)

question.answer: (a) Shown. (b) $(-2, 2)$, a minimum point, and $(-2, -2)$, a maximum point ($\frac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2} = \frac{1}{y} = \pm\frac{1}{2}$ there). (c) No point of $C$ has a tangent through the origin: the condition forces $x^2 = 3y^2$, which contradicts $x(x^2 - 3y^2) = 16$.
skills: implicit differentiation of the cubic curve $x^3 - 3xy^2 = 16$, where $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = 0$ gives the pair of lines $y = \pm x$ and both must be followed back to the curve (one real $x$, two points)

nature of the stationary points of an implicit curve by differentiating the implicit relation a second time with $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = 0$ substituted ($\frac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2} = \frac{1}{y}$): a maximum point that lies below a minimum point, on different branches

deciding whether any tangent to an implicit curve passes through a given point (the origin): the condition $y = x\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$ reduces to $x^2 = 3y^2$, which contradicts the curve's equation, with the tangent parallel to the $y$-axis checked separately
question.solution:
(a) Differentiating $x^3 - 3xy^2 = 16$ implicitly with respect to $x$ (product rule on $3xy^2$):
$3x^2 - 3y^2 - 6xy\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = 0$
$6xy\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = 3x^2 - 3y^2$
$\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \frac{x^2 - y^2}{2xy}$ (shown).

(b) No point of $C$ has $x = 0$ (it gives $0 = 16$).
For a stationary point, $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = 0$, so $x^2 - y^2 = 0$ with $xy \neq 0$, i.e. $y = x$ or $y = -x$.
In either case $y^2 = x^2$, so the equation of $C$ gives $x^3 - 3x^3 = -2x^3 = 16$, so $x^3 = -8$ and $x = -2$ (the only real root).
Then $y = \pm 2$: the stationary points are $(-2, 2)$ and $(-2, -2)$. At both, $2xy = \mp 8 \neq 0$, so $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$ is defined and equal to 0 there.
Nature: write the result of (a) as $2xy\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = x^2 - y^2$ and differentiate again with respect to $x$:
$2y\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} + 2x\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\right)^2 + 2xy\frac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2} = 2x - 2y\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$.
At a stationary point $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = 0$, so $2xy\frac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2} = 2x$, i.e. $\frac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2} = \frac{1}{y}$.
At $(-2, 2)$: $\frac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2} = \frac{1}{2} > 0$, so $(-2, 2)$ is a minimum point.
At $(-2, -2)$: $\frac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2} = -\frac{1}{2} < 0$, so $(-2, -2)$ is a maximum point.
[The maximum point lies below the minimum point. $C$ is symmetric in the $x$-axis, and for $x < 0$ it has two separate branches: for $x < 0$, $y^2 = \frac{x^3 - 16}{3x} = \frac{x^2}{3} - \frac{16}{3x}$, whose least value on $x < 0$ is $4$, at $x = -2$. So the branch with $y > 0$ has lowest point $(-2, 2)$ and the branch with $y < 0$ has highest point $(-2, -2)$.]

(c) Let $P(p, q)$ be any point on $C$, so $p^3 - 3pq^2 = p(p^2 - 3q^2) = 16$; in particular $p \neq 0$.
Tangent parallel to the $y$-axis: $2pq = 0$, so $q = 0$ and $p^3 = 16$, giving the point $(\sqrt[3]{16}, 0)$; its tangent $x = \sqrt[3]{16}$ does not pass through $O$.
Otherwise $q \neq 0$, and the tangent at $P$ is $y - q = m(x - p)$, where $m = \frac{p^2 - q^2}{2pq}$. It passes through $O(0, 0)$ if and only if $-q = -mp$, i.e. $q = mp = \frac{p^2 - q^2}{2q}$.
So $2q^2 = p^2 - q^2$, i.e. $p^2 = 3q^2$.
But then $p^3 - 3pq^2 = p(p^2 - 3q^2) = 0 \neq 16$, so $P$ would not lie on $C$ — a contradiction.
Hence there is no point on $C$ at which the tangent to $C$ passes through the origin.
[The lines $y = \pm\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}}$ through $O$ are asymptotes of $C$; the tangents approach them but none passes through $O$.]
question.syllabus_check: 9758 Differentiation only: implicit differentiation (product rule); stationary points and their nature by the second-derivative test, the second derivative obtained by differentiating the implicit relation again; tangents to an implicit curve, including one parallel to the $y$-axis, and whether a tangent passes through a given point — all in the 9758 differentiation content. No parametric second derivative, no non-stationary point of inflexion, no Maclaurin series, no modelled maximum. No calculator needed; every value exact and integer or simple fraction ($\sqrt[3]{16}$ appears only as the position of the vertical tangent).
question.originality_note: New curve $x^3 - 3xy^2 = 16$ (a homogeneous cubic set equal to a constant, symmetric in the $x$-axis, three branches), replacing the curve of GCE 2014 P1 Q2 ($x^2y + xy^2 + 54 = 0$), which the moderator found lifted. Not GCE 2014 P1 Q2 (the one point where the gradient is $-1$), GCE 2017 P1 Q3 (exact stationary points of the conic $y^2 - 2xy + 5x^2 = 10$, nature at one) or GCE 2018 P1 Q7 (two tangents at $x = 1$ meeting at $N$): here $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = 0$ gives a pair of lines, both followed to the curve; the two stationary points share an $x$-coordinate and have opposite natures, the maximum below the minimum; and the last part is a decision, closed by a contradiction, about tangents through the origin. Differs from our Set 1 P1 Q3 (a $\tan^{-1}$ function with zero derivative), Set 1 P1 Q7 ($\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \sin 2y$ then a Maclaurin series), Set 1 P1 Q6 (stationary points of an explicit rational curve, then $\mathrm{f}(|x|) = k$) and Set 1 P1 Q8 (perpendicular tangents to a parametric curve): no sketch, no set of values of $k$, no parametric curve.

answers.(b): (-2, 2) is a minimum point (d2y/dx2 = 1/2 > 0); (-2, -2) is a maximum point (d2y/dx2 = -1/2 < 0)
answers.(c): No such point. Tangent at (x, y) passes through O iff y = x(dy/dx), i.e. 2y^2 = x^2 - y^2, so x^2 = 3y^2; then x^3 - 3xy^2 = x^3 - x^3 = 0, not 16, a contradiction. (The vertical tangent at (16^(1/3), 0) is x = 16^(1/3), which does not pass through O; x = 0 is never on C.)

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both 'shown'. Re-derived: 3x^2 - 3y^2 - 6xy dy/dx = 0, so dy/dx = (x^2 - y^2)/(2xy). Correct; xy = 0 never occurs on C (x = 0 gives 0 = 16; y = 0 gives the single point (16^(1/3), 0), where the tangent is vertical, not stationary).

parts.label: (b)
parts.note: Both give (-2, 2) a minimum and (-2, -2) a maximum. Confirmed: dy/dx = 0 forces y^2 = x^2, then -2x^3 = 16 gives the one real x = -2 and y = +/-2. Differentiating 2xy dy/dx = x^2 - y^2 again and putting dy/dx = 0 gives 2xy d2y/dx2 = 2x, so d2y/dx2 = 1/y: +1/2 at (-2, 2), -1/2 at (-2, -2). Cross-checked on the explicit branches: for x < 0, y^2 = x^2/3 - 16/(3x) has derivative 2x/3 + 16/(3x^2) = 0 at x = -2 and second derivative 2/3 + 4/3 = 2 > 0, so y^2 is least (= 4) there; the upper branch has its lowest point at (-2, 2) and the lower branch its highest at (-2, -2). The maximum below the minimum is genuine, not a slip.

parts.label: (c)
parts.note: Both conclude no such point, by the same argument, and it is right: the tangent at (p, q) passes through O iff q = p dy/dx; with q != 0 this is 2q^2 = p^2 - q^2, i.e. p^2 = 3q^2, and then p^3 - 3pq^2 = p(p^2 - 3q^2) = 0 != 16. The only vertical tangent, x = 16^(1/3) at (16^(1/3), 0), misses O. No singular point exists (numerator and denominator vanish together only at (0, 0), which is not on C). Confirmed independently: F = x^3 - 3xy^2 is homogeneous of degree 3, so p F_x + q F_y = 3F(p, q) = 48 != 0 at every point of C, which is exactly the condition for the tangent to miss the origin.

verdict.key_verdict: No disagreement: the setter and the blind examiner agree on all three parts and each is confirmed by independent working, including the maximum point (-2, -2) lying below the minimum point (-2, 2) on different branches.
verdict.why: A clean implicit-curve question at the 2022-2024 standard for 9 marks in the Q2 slot: (a) is a standard derivation that gates (b) and (c); (b) makes the candidate follow both lines y = +/-x back to the curve and decide the nature of stationary points on an implicit curve by a second implicit differentiation, with a maximum that sits below a minimum as the twist; (c) is the idea the candidate must supply - turning 'the tangent passes through O' into y = x dy/dx, reducing it to x^2 = 3y^2 and closing the non-existence proof against the curve's own equation, with the vertical tangent disposed of - one idea, in about six minutes, and no part carries two. The first-round objection is answered: x^3 - 3xy^2 = 16 is a different polynomial from GCE 2014 P1 Q2's x^2 y + xy^2 + 54 = 0 and the parts ask different things (stationary points and nature, then a tangent through O, not a gradient -1 point), the novelty gate passes (Jaccard 0.11), GCE 2024 P1 Q6(b)(i) uses a tangent through the origin only to fix a constant on an explicit curve, and no 2022-2024 Paper 2 question is an implicit curve. Nothing in Set 1 P1 tests these skills (Q7's implicit step feeds a Maclaurin series, Q6's stationary points are on an explicit rational function, Q8's tangents are parametric), nothing in this paper so far does (Q4 is connected rates), the setter's skills phrases are true and specific, and the marks match the work (2 + 4 + 3).

question.stem:
The function $\mathrm{f}$ is defined by
$\mathrm{f}: x \mapsto \mathrm{e}^{x} + 4\mathrm{e}^{-x}, \quad x \in \mathbb{R},\ x \geqslant a,$
where $a$ is a constant.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Find the least value of $a$ for which the function $\mathrm{f}^{-1}$ exists, giving your answer in exact form.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: It is now given that $a$ takes the value found in part (a). Find $\mathrm{f}^{-1}(x)$ and state the domain of $\mathrm{f}^{-1}$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Sketch, on the same diagram, the graphs of $y = \mathrm{f}(x)$ and $y = \mathrm{f}^{-1}(x)$, stating the exact coordinates of the end-point of each graph. Explain why the equation $\mathrm{f}(x) = \mathrm{f}^{-1}(x)$ has no solution.
parts.answer: Sketch: $y = \mathrm{f}(x)$ starts at $(\ln 2, 4)$, increasing and concave upward; $y = \mathrm{f}^{-1}(x)$ is its reflection in $y = x$, starting at $(4, \ln 2)$, increasing and concave downward. Since $\mathrm{e}^{x} - x \geqslant 1$ and $4\mathrm{e}^{-x} > 0$, $\mathrm{f}(x) > x$ for all $x \geqslant \ln 2$, so the graph of $\mathrm{f}$ lies entirely above $y = x$ and its reflection, the graph of $\mathrm{f}^{-1}$, lies entirely below $y = x$; the graphs never meet, so $\mathrm{f}(x) = \mathrm{f}^{-1}(x)$ has no solution.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: The function $\mathrm{g}$ is defined by $\mathrm{g}: x \mapsto k + \mathrm{e}^{-x}, \ x \in \mathbb{R}$, where $k$ is a constant.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.text: Find the set of values of $k$ for which the composite function $\mathrm{fg}$ exists.

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.text: For these values of $k$, find the range of $\mathrm{fg}$, giving your answer in terms of $k$.

question.answer: (a) $a = \ln 2$. (b) $\mathrm{f}^{-1}(x) = \ln\left(\frac{x + \sqrt{x^2 - 16}}{2}\right)$, domain $x \geqslant 4$. (c) Sketch with end-points $(\ln 2, 4)$ on $y = \mathrm{f}(x)$ and $(4, \ln 2)$ on $y = \mathrm{f}^{-1}(x)$; $\mathrm{f}(x) > x$ for all $x \geqslant \ln 2$, so the graph of $\mathrm{f}$ is above $y = x$, the graph of $\mathrm{f}^{-1}$ below it, and they never meet. (d)(i) $k \geqslant \ln 2$. (d)(ii) $\left(\mathrm{e}^{k} + 4\mathrm{e}^{-k}, \infty\right)$.
skills: inverse of a function that is quadratic in $\mathrm{e}^{x}$, the root chosen by the restricted domain ($\mathrm{e}^{x} \geqslant 2$) because both roots are positive
explaining why $y = \mathrm{f}(x)$ and $y = \mathrm{f}^{-1}(x)$ never meet from $\mathrm{f}(x) > x$ (graph above $y = x$, its reflection below)
existence of $\mathrm{fg}$ with a parameter: an open range $(k, \infty)$ inside the closed domain $[\ln 2, \infty)$ with the boundary value included, and the range of $\mathrm{fg}$ in terms of $k$
question.solution:
(a) $\mathrm{f}'(x) = \mathrm{e}^{x} - 4\mathrm{e}^{-x}$. $\mathrm{f}'(x) = 0 \iff \mathrm{e}^{2x} = 4 \iff x = \ln 2$. [M1]
$\mathrm{f}''(x) = \mathrm{e}^{x} + 4\mathrm{e}^{-x} > 0$, so the curve has a minimum point at $(\ln 2, \mathrm{f}(\ln 2)) = (\ln 2, 2 + 2) = (\ln 2, 4)$: $\mathrm{f}$ is strictly decreasing for $x < \ln 2$ and strictly increasing for $x > \ln 2$.
If $a < \ln 2$, the domain contains points on both sides of $x = \ln 2$ with the same value of $\mathrm{f}$ (a horizontal line $y = c$ with $4 < c \leqslant \mathrm{f}(a)$ meets the graph twice), so $\mathrm{f}$ is not one-one and $\mathrm{f}^{-1}$ does not exist. If $a \geqslant \ln 2$, $\mathrm{f}$ is strictly increasing, hence one-one.
Least value of $a$ is $\ln 2$. [A1]

(b) Let $y = \mathrm{e}^{x} + 4\mathrm{e}^{-x}$, $x \geqslant \ln 2$. Multiplying by $\mathrm{e}^{x}$: $(\mathrm{e}^{x})^2 - y\,\mathrm{e}^{x} + 4 = 0$, so $\mathrm{e}^{x} = \frac{y \pm \sqrt{y^2 - 16}}{2}$. [M1]
Both roots are positive (their product is 4), so $\mathrm{e}^{x} > 0$ does not decide between them. The domain gives $x \geqslant \ln 2$, i.e. $\mathrm{e}^{x} \geqslant 2$. Since the two roots have product 4, the smaller root $\frac{y - \sqrt{y^2 - 16}}{2}$ is less than 2 whenever $y > 4$ (the roots are equal, both 2, only when $y = 4$). So the minus sign is rejected and $\mathrm{e}^{x} = \frac{y + \sqrt{y^2 - 16}}{2}$, $x = \ln\left(\frac{y + \sqrt{y^2 - 16}}{2}\right)$. [A1, with the reason for the rejection]
Hence $\mathrm{f}^{-1}(x) = \ln\left(\frac{x + \sqrt{x^2 - 16}}{2}\right)$.
$D_{\mathrm{f}^{-1}} = R_{\mathrm{f}}$: $\mathrm{f}$ increases from $\mathrm{f}(\ln 2) = 4$ and $\mathrm{f}(x) \to \infty$ as $x \to \infty$, so $D_{\mathrm{f}^{-1}} = [4, \infty)$. [B1]
Check: $\mathrm{f}^{-1}(5) = \ln\frac{5 + 3}{2} = \ln 4$ and $\mathrm{f}(\ln 4) = 4 + 1 = 5$.

(c) Sketch: $y = \mathrm{f}(x)$ begins at the end-point $(\ln 2, 4)$ and rises, concave upward ($\mathrm{f}''(x) > 0$), without bound. [B1]
$y = \mathrm{f}^{-1}(x)$ is the reflection of $y = \mathrm{f}(x)$ in the line $y = x$: it begins at the end-point $(4, \ln 2)$ and rises, concave downward, without bound (the line $y = x$ may be drawn as the mirror line). [B1]
Explanation: for every real $x$, $\mathrm{e}^{x} - x \geqslant 1$ (the least value of $\mathrm{e}^{x} - x$ is 1, at $x = 0$), so $\mathrm{f}(x) - x = (\mathrm{e}^{x} - x) + 4\mathrm{e}^{-x} > 0$, i.e. $\mathrm{f}(x) > x$ for all $x \geqslant \ln 2$. The graph of $\mathrm{f}$ therefore lies entirely above the line $y = x$, so its reflection in $y = x$, the graph of $\mathrm{f}^{-1}$, lies entirely below that line. The two graphs have no common point, so $\mathrm{f}(x) = \mathrm{f}^{-1}(x)$ has no solution. [B1]
(Equivalently: $\mathrm{f}$ is increasing, so a point common to both graphs would lie on $y = x$ and satisfy $\mathrm{f}(x) = x$, which is impossible since $\mathrm{f}(x) > x$.)

(d)(i) As $x$ ranges over $\mathbb{R}$, $\mathrm{e}^{-x}$ takes every value in $(0, \infty)$, so $R_{\mathrm{g}} = (k, \infty)$. [B1]
$\mathrm{fg}$ exists $\iff R_{\mathrm{g}} \subseteq D_{\mathrm{f}} = [\ln 2, \infty) \iff k \geqslant \ln 2$. The value $k = \ln 2$ is included: then $R_{\mathrm{g}} = (\ln 2, \infty)$, which lies inside $[\ln 2, \infty)$. Set of values: $\{k \in \mathbb{R} : k \geqslant \ln 2\}$. [A1]

(d)(ii) For $k \geqslant \ln 2$, $\mathrm{g}$ maps $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(k, \infty) \subseteq [\ln 2, \infty)$, on which $\mathrm{f}$ is strictly increasing and unbounded. Since $\mathrm{g}(x)$ never equals $k$, the value $\mathrm{f}(k)$ is not attained: $R_{\mathrm{fg}} = (\mathrm{f}(k), \infty) = \left(\mathrm{e}^{k} + 4\mathrm{e}^{-k}, \infty\right)$. [B1]
(For example, $k = \ln 2$ gives $(4, \infty)$, which is not the range $[4, \infty)$ of $\mathrm{f}$.)
question.syllabus_check: 9758 Functions: restricting a domain so that an inverse exists (least $a$ from the minimum point, found by differentiation, an A Math skill assumed), finding $\mathrm{f}^{-1}(x)$ with the domain of $\mathrm{f}^{-1}$ as the range of $\mathrm{f}$, the graph of $\mathrm{f}^{-1}$ as the reflection of $\mathrm{f}$ in $y = x$, the condition $R_{\mathrm{g}} \subseteq D_{\mathrm{f}}$ for $\mathrm{fg}$ to exist and the range of a composite. Solving a quadratic in $\mathrm{e}^{x}$ is assumed O-Level A Math knowledge. No $(\mathrm{fg})^{-1}$, no domain restricted to make a composite exist (the parameter is in g's rule, not a restriction of a domain), no figure printed, no calculator ban; a graphing calculator helps with the sketch but every answer is exact.
question.originality_note: New function and new sequence. Real papers restrict a quadratic (GCE 2025 specimen P2 Q1, GCE 2024 P2 Q3), $\frac{1}{1-x^2}$ (GCE 2015 P2 Q3), a modulus rational (GCE 2023 P1 Q7) or a log (GCE 2011 P2 Q3); here the function is quadratic in $\mathrm{e}^{x}$ and the inverse needs a root chosen by $\mathrm{e}^{x} \geqslant 2$ with BOTH roots positive. Where GCE 2011 P2 Q3 and GCE 2008 P2 Q4 solve $\mathrm{f}(x) = \mathrm{f}^{-1}(x)$ on $y = x$, this question reverses it: the candidate must explain why there is NO solution. The composite part carries a parameter in g and asks for the existence condition with an open range meeting a closed domain, then the range in terms of $k$ (GCE 2013 P2 Q1 only asks why fg does not exist). Set 1 P1 Q3 tested a constant $\tan^{-1}$ function by a zero derivative, and Set 1 P1 Q6 a rational curve with $\mathrm{f}(|x|)$; neither asks for an inverse, a reflection or a composite.

answers.(a): a = ln 2 (f'(x) = e^x - 4e^{-x} = 0 at x = ln 2, the minimum point (ln 2, 4))
answers.(c): Sketch: y = f(x) increasing from end-point (ln 2, 4); y = f^{-1}(x) its reflection in y = x, increasing from end-point (4, ln 2). No solution: f is increasing and f(x) > e^x > x for all x ≥ ln 2, so the graph of y = f(x) lies entirely above y = x; any intersection of y = f(x) and y = f^{-1}(x) (f increasing) would have to lie on y = x, so the graphs never meet and f(x) = f^{-1}(x) has no solution.
answers.(d)(i): R_g = (k, ∞) must be a subset of D_f = [ln 2, ∞): {k ∈ R : k ≥ ln 2}

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both give a = ln 2: f'(x) = e^x - 4e^{-x} = 0 at e^{2x} = 4, the minimum point (ln 2, 4); f is one-one exactly when the domain starts at or after it. Checked.

parts.label: (b)
parts.note: Both give f^{-1}(x) = ln((x + sqrt(x^2 - 16))/2) with domain [4, infinity). Checked: u = e^x satisfies u^2 - yu + 4 = 0, both roots positive with product 4, so for y > 4 the smaller root is below 2 and the domain e^x >= 2 forces the plus sign; f^{-1}(5) = ln 4 and f(ln 4) = 5.

parts.label: (c)
parts.note: Same sketch (f from end-point (ln 2, 4), concave up; f^{-1} its reflection from (4, ln 2)) and the same argument in two dressings: setter uses e^x - x >= 1, examiner uses e^x > x; either gives f(x) > x on the whole domain, so the graph of f is above y = x, its reflection below, and they never meet. Valid.

parts.label: (d)(i)
parts.note: Both give {k : k >= ln 2}. Checked: R_g = (k, infinity) is open, so k = ln 2 is admitted by the closed domain [ln 2, infinity) of f.

parts.label: (d)(ii)
parts.note: Both give R_fg = (e^k + 4e^{-k}, infinity). Checked: f is strictly increasing and unbounded on (k, infinity) for k >= ln 2, and f(k) itself is never attained because g never equals k.

question.stem: A fuel tank is a closed cylinder of internal radius $1$ m and internal length $5$ m. The tank lies with its axis horizontal. The diagram shows the circular cross-section of the tank, with centre $O$, when the depth of fuel in the tank is $h$ m. The surface of the fuel meets this cross-section in the line $AB$, and $\theta$ radians is the angle subtended at $O$ by the arc of the circle that is in contact with the fuel, where $0 < \theta < 2\pi$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Show that, for $0 < \theta < \pi$, $h = 1 - \cos\frac{1}{2}\theta$ and the volume of fuel in the tank, $V$ m$^3$, is given by $V = \frac{5}{2}(\theta - \sin\theta)$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
It is given that both results in part (a) are also true for $\pi \le \theta < 2\pi$.
Fuel is pumped into the tank at a constant rate of $0.3$ m$^3$ per minute, starting when the depth of fuel is $0.5$ m. At time $t$ minutes after pumping starts, the depth of fuel is $h$ m.
Find the rate at which the area of the horizontal surface of the fuel is increasing at the instant when pumping starts.

parts.label: (c)
parts.answer: (i) Shown; (ii) least rate $0.03$ m per minute, when the depth of fuel is $1$ m

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.text: Hence find the least rate at which the depth of fuel increases, and state the depth of fuel when this occurs.
subparts.answer: $0.03$ m per minute, when the depth of fuel is $1$ m (the tank is half full)

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Find the depth of fuel at the instant when the depth is increasing at a rate of $0.06$ m per minute. Find also the exact time taken from the start of pumping to this instant.
parts.answer: Depth $= 1 + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ m $(\approx 1.87$ m$)$; time $= \frac{25}{3}(\pi + \sqrt{3})$ minutes $(\approx 40.6$ minutes$)$

question.answer: (a) Shown. (b) $0.2$ m$^2$ per minute. (c)(i) Shown. (c)(ii) $0.03$ m per minute, when the depth of fuel is $1$ m. (d) Depth $1 + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ m $(\approx 1.87$ m$)$; time $\frac{25}{3}(\pi + \sqrt{3})$ minutes $(\approx 40.6$ minutes$)$.
skills: volume of liquid in a horizontal cylinder built as sector minus triangle in terms of the angle subtended by the wetted arc, with the depth from the half-angle
connected rates through an angle parameter: the rate of change of the liquid's surface area, and the depth's rate as a cosec expression whose least value is at half-full
two depths with the same rate of rise, the one below the starting depth rejected by the context, then an exact time from the volume between two angles
question.figure_description: The circular cross-section of the tank only (no 3-D view). A circle about 6 cm across; its centre is marked with a dot and labelled O. A horizontal chord AB is drawn BELOW O, positioned so that angle AOB is about 120 degrees (A at the left end of the chord, B at the right end). The radii OA and OB are drawn as straight lines, and OA is labelled 1 m. The region of the circle below the chord AB (the fuel) is shaded. The angle AOB between OA and OB, on the side facing the shaded region (the angle that opens downwards towards the lowest point of the circle), is marked with a small arc at O and labelled θ. A vertical double-headed arrow runs from the lowest point of the circle up to the chord AB and is labelled h m. No other labels: no numerical value of θ or h, no formula for the volume or for h, no axes, no length of the tank.
question.solution:
(a) In the cross-section the fuel occupies the segment of the circle cut off by the chord $AB$ and bounded by the arc in contact with the fuel. For $0 < \theta < \pi$ this segment is the sector $OAB$ of angle $\theta$ minus the triangle $OAB$.
Area of sector $= \frac{1}{2}(1)^2\theta = \frac{1}{2}\theta$; area of triangle $OAB = \frac{1}{2}(1)(1)\sin\theta = \frac{1}{2}\sin\theta$.
Area of fuel in the cross-section $= \frac{1}{2}(\theta - \sin\theta)$ m$^2$. The tank has a uniform cross-section and length $5$ m, so $V = 5 \times \frac{1}{2}(\theta - \sin\theta) = \frac{5}{2}(\theta - \sin\theta)$.
The perpendicular from $O$ to $AB$ bisects angle $AOB$, so the distance from $O$ to $AB$ is $1 \times \cos\frac{1}{2}\theta$. The lowest point of the cross-section is $1$ m below $O$, so $h = 1 - \cos\frac{1}{2}\theta$.
(b) When pumping starts, $h = 0.5$, so $\cos\frac{1}{2}\theta = \frac{1}{2}$, $\frac{1}{2}\theta = \frac{\pi}{3}$, $\theta = \frac{2\pi}{3}$.
$\frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}\theta} = \frac{5}{2}(1 - \cos\theta)$; at $\theta = \frac{2\pi}{3}$ this is $\frac{5}{2}\left(1 + \frac{1}{2}\right) = \frac{15}{4}$.
$\frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}\theta}\frac{\mathrm{d}\theta}{\mathrm{d}t}$ gives $0.3 = \frac{15}{4}\frac{\mathrm{d}\theta}{\mathrm{d}t}$, so $\frac{\mathrm{d}\theta}{\mathrm{d}t} = 0.08$ rad per minute.
The surface of the fuel is a rectangle of length $5$ m and width $AB = 2\sin\frac{1}{2}\theta$ m, so its area is $S = 10\sin\frac{1}{2}\theta$.
$\frac{\mathrm{d}S}{\mathrm{d}t} = 5\cos\frac{1}{2}\theta \cdot \frac{\mathrm{d}\theta}{\mathrm{d}t} = 5 \times \frac{1}{2} \times 0.08 = 0.2$ m$^2$ per minute.
(c)(i) $\frac{\mathrm{d}\theta}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{0.3}{\frac{5}{2}(1 - \cos\theta)} = \frac{0.12}{1 - \cos\theta} = \frac{0.12}{2\sin^2\frac{1}{2}\theta} = \frac{0.06}{\sin^2\frac{1}{2}\theta}$.
$\frac{\mathrm{d}h}{\mathrm{d}\theta} = \frac{1}{2}\sin\frac{1}{2}\theta$, so $\frac{\mathrm{d}h}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{1}{2}\sin\frac{1}{2}\theta \times \frac{0.06}{\sin^2\frac{1}{2}\theta} = \frac{0.03}{\sin\frac{1}{2}\theta} = \frac{3}{100}\operatorname{cosec}\frac{1}{2}\theta$.
(c)(ii) For $0 < \theta < 2\pi$, $0 < \sin\frac{1}{2}\theta \le 1$, so $\frac{\mathrm{d}h}{\mathrm{d}t} \ge 0.03$, with equality when $\frac{1}{2}\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}$, i.e. $\theta = \pi$ and $h = 1 - \cos\frac{\pi}{2} = 1$. Least rate $0.03$ m per minute, when the depth is $1$ m (the tank is half full, where the surface is widest).
(d) $\frac{3}{100}\operatorname{cosec}\frac{1}{2}\theta = 0.06 \Rightarrow \sin\frac{1}{2}\theta = \frac{1}{2}$. Since $0 < \frac{1}{2}\theta < \pi$, $\frac{1}{2}\theta = \frac{\pi}{6}$ or $\frac{5\pi}{6}$, so $\theta = \frac{\pi}{3}$ or $\frac{5\pi}{3}$.
$\theta = \frac{\pi}{3}$ gives $h = 1 - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \approx 0.134$ m, which is less than $0.5$ m; the depth only increases from $0.5$ m once pumping starts, so this depth never occurs after pumping starts and is rejected.
So $\theta = \frac{5\pi}{3}$ and $h = 1 - \cos\frac{5\pi}{6} = 1 + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \approx 1.87$ m (less than $2$ m, so the tank is not yet full).
Volume pumped in $= \frac{5}{2}\left(\frac{5\pi}{3} - \sin\frac{5\pi}{3}\right) - \frac{5}{2}\left(\frac{2\pi}{3} - \sin\frac{2\pi}{3}\right) = \frac{5}{2}\left[\left(\frac{5\pi}{3} + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) - \left(\frac{2\pi}{3} - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\right] = \frac{5}{2}(\pi + \sqrt{3})$ m$^3$.
Time $= \frac{\frac{5}{2}(\pi + \sqrt{3})}{0.3} = \frac{25}{3}(\pi + \sqrt{3})$ minutes $\approx 40.6$ minutes.

question.stem: Ten people, including Mr Lim and Mrs Lim, are to be seated at two round tables, one with 6 seats and the other with 4 seats. At each table, seating arrangements that are rotations of one another are regarded as the same.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Find the number of different ways in which the 10 people can be seated.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Find the number of ways in which the 10 people can be seated so that Mr Lim and Mrs Lim sit next to each other.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: The 10 people are seated at random. Given that Mr Lim and Mrs Lim sit at the same table, find the probability that they do not sit next to each other.

skills: seating at two round tables of different sizes: choosing who sits at each table, then a circular arrangement at each (the tables are distinguishable, so no division by 2)
a pair next to each other at a round table, split into cases by which table the pair shares, with the pair treated as one unit and the companions chosen first
conditional probability from counted arrangements: P(not adjacent | same table) = P(same table, not adjacent) / P(same table)
question.solution:
(a) Choose the 6 guests who sit at the 6-seat table: $\binom{10}{6} = 210$ ways; the other 4 sit at the 4-seat table.
Arrangements round the 6-seat table: $(6-1)! = 120$. Arrangements round the 4-seat table: $(4-1)! = 6$.
Number of ways $= 210 \times 120 \times 6 = 151\,200$. [M1 A1]

(b) If Mr and Mrs Lim sit next to each other they sit at the same table. Two cases.
Case 1: both at the 6-seat table. Choose the other 4 guests at that table from the remaining 8: $\binom{8}{4} = 70$. Treat the couple as one unit: 5 units round the table in $(5-1)! = 24$ ways, and the couple can be arranged in $2! = 2$ ways within the unit, giving $48$. The other 4 guests round the 4-seat table: $3! = 6$.
Case 1 total $= 70 \times 48 \times 6 = 20\,160$. [M1]
Case 2: both at the 4-seat table. Choose the other 2 guests at that table from the remaining 8: $\binom{8}{2} = 28$. Couple as one unit: 3 units round the table in $(3-1)! = 2$ ways, $\times 2$ within the unit, giving $4$. The other 6 guests round the 6-seat table: $5! = 120$.
Case 2 total $= 28 \times 4 \times 120 = 13\,440$. [M1]
Number of ways $= 20\,160 + 13\,440 = 33\,600$. [A1]

(c) Number of ways in which they sit at the same table:
both at the 6-seat table: $\binom{8}{4} \times 5! \times 3! = 70 \times 720 = 50\,400$;
both at the 4-seat table: $\binom{8}{2} \times 5! \times 3! = 28 \times 720 = 20\,160$;
total $= 70\,560$.
Sitting next to each other is contained in sitting at the same table, so the number of ways in which they sit at the same table but not next to each other is $70\,560 - 33\,600 = 36\,960$. [M1]
Required probability $= \frac{36\,960}{151\,200} = \frac{11}{45}$ $(0.244)$. [A1]
Alternatively: $\mathrm{P}(\text{same table}) = \frac{6}{10} \times \frac{5}{9} + \frac{4}{10} \times \frac{3}{9} = \frac{7}{15}$ and $\mathrm{P}(\text{next to each other}) = \frac{33\,600}{151\,200} = \frac{2}{9}$, so the probability is $\frac{7}{15} - \frac{2}{9} = \frac{21 - 10}{45} = \frac{11}{45}$.
(Check by direct count: at the 4-seat table 'not next to each other' means opposite each other, $28 \times 2 \times 120 = 6720$; at the 6-seat table $70 \times (120 - 48) \times 6 = 30\,240$; total $36\,960$.)
All three counts were confirmed by a complete enumeration of the $10!$ seatings of labelled seats, divided by $6 \times 4$ rotations.

(c) [revised at moderation] P(same table) = [C(8,4)·5!·3! + C(8,2)·5!·3!]/151 200 = (50 400 + 20 160)/151 200 = 7/15. P(same table and next to each other) = 33 600/151 200 = 2/9. So P(same table, not next to each other) = 7/15 − 2/9 = 11/45, and P(not next to each other | same table) = (11/45)/(7/15) = 11/21 ≈ 0.524. M1 for the conditioning event P(same table) = 7/15 (or the count 70 560), A1 for 11/21.
question.syllabus_check: 9758 Section B, Permutations and Combinations: arrangements in a circle with a restriction (two people together, treated as a unit), selection of who sits at each table (combinations), the multiplication and addition principles over cases; Probability: a probability from counting and P(A and not B) = P(A) - P(B) when B is contained in A. No figure, no calculator needed beyond arithmetic, nothing outside the syllabus (no identical tables, no reflections/bracelets, no identical objects in a circle).
question.originality_note: No GCE question from 2008 to 2025 seats people at two tables. The circular questions in the corpus seat one group round a single table or circle (GCE 2016 P2 Q7(iii)-(iv), three officers adjacent or separated round one table of 10; GCE 2012 P2 Q7(v), sisters adjacent in one circle for 1 mark; GCE 2017 P2 Q6(iii), father cards separated in a circle). The exemplars are a row of digit cards (GCE 2025 P2 Q7), committees with conditions (GCE 2022 P2 Q7, GCE 2024 P2 Q6) and ratio-of-probability counters/shapes questions (GCE 2023 P2 Q6, GCE 2020 P2 Q8); none shares this situation or its sequence of parts. No earlier Set has a Permutations and Combinations question, and this paper's other slots put conditional probability and independence in Q9, so part (c) deliberately asks for a difference of probabilities, not a conditional one. The decision that carries the standard is splitting by which table the couple shares (different table sizes give different block counts, and at the 4-seat table 'not next to each other' can only mean opposite).

parts.note: Both 151 200. Re-derived: C(10,6) x 5! x 3! = 210 x 120 x 6 = 151 200; the two tables differ in size so they are distinguishable and there is no division by 2.

parts.label: (b)
parts.note: Both 33 600. Re-derived: 6-seat table C(8,4) x 4! x 2 x 3! = 20 160; 4-seat table C(8,2) x 2! x 2 x 5! = 13 440; sum 33 600. Cross-checked as a probability: 6/10 x 5/9 x 2/5 + 4/10 x 3/9 x 2/3 = 2/15 + 4/45 = 2/9 = 33 600 / 151 200.

parts.label: (c)
parts.note: Both 11/45 (0.244). Re-derived: P(same table) = 6/10 x 5/9 + 4/10 x 3/9 = 7/15; 7/15 - 2/9 = 11/45. Direct count agrees: 6/10 x 5/9 x 3/5 + 4/10 x 3/9 x 1/3 = 9/45 + 2/45 = 11/45 (at the 4-seat table 'not next to each other' means opposite).

verdict.key_verdict: The setter and the blind examiner agree on every part, and my own working confirms all three values (151 200; 33 600; 11/45), so the key is right.
fixes: Close on a conditional probability, the way the 2022-2024 starters close (GCE 2022 P2 Q6(b) 'Given that Babs wins', 2025 P2 Q7(d) 'Given that the even digits are all together'): replace (c) with 'The 10 guests are seated at random. Given that Mr Lim and Mrs Lim sit at the same table, find the probability that they do not sit next to each other.' [2] - key 11/21 (= (11/45) / (7/15)); the candidate must then supply P(same table) = 7/15 as the conditioning event rather than only subtract the answer to (b) from it.

Register: SEAB would open 'Ten people, including Mr and Mrs Lim, are to be seated at two round tables, one with 6 seats and the other with 4 seats.' - drop 'at a dinner', 'a married couple' and 'and every seat is taken' (10 guests fill 10 seats, so the sentence adds nothing); keep the rotations sentence.

For the session, not a rejection: no words are asked for anywhere, which standard.md section 5 item 10 lists as a question-level anti-pattern. I have not rejected on it because the 2022-2024 counting and probability starters this slot is measured against (GCE 2022 P2 Q6, GCE 2023 P2 Q6, GCE 2024 P2 Q7) ask for none either, so the rule as written would reject those real questions; but this slot contributes zero explain units, so Section B's 4-11 must come entirely from Q6-Q10, or a one-mark reason in context is added here.

It is a familiar tutorial configuration that closes one notch plainer than a GCE starter (no conditional, no words), so a real question after a light edit rather than indistinguishable from one.

question.stem: An airline operates a flight which has 180 seats for passengers. On average, $5\%$ of the people who have bought a ticket for this flight do not turn up for it, so the airline sells more than 180 tickets for each flight. The number of ticket-holders who turn up for a randomly chosen flight is denoted by $X$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State, in context, two assumptions needed for $X$ to be well modelled by a binomial distribution.
parts.answer: Whether a ticket-holder turns up for the flight is independent of whether any other ticket-holder turns up; the probability that a ticket-holder turns up is the same for every ticket-holder.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Explain why one of these assumptions may not be reasonable for the people who buy tickets for this flight.
parts.answer: People who buy tickets together and travel as a group (a family or a tour group) tend either all to turn up or all not to turn up, so ticket-holders do not turn up independently of one another. (Or: the probability of turning up differs between ticket-holders, e.g. business travellers with flexible tickets are more likely to change flights than holidaymakers.)

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Assume now that $X$ has a binomial distribution. The airline sells 184 tickets for each of the 7 flights on this route in a randomly chosen week. Find the probability that, on at least 2 of these 7 flights, a ticket-holder who turns up cannot be given a seat. State the distribution you use.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: The airline wants the probability that every ticket-holder who turns up for a flight can be given a seat to be at least $0.95$. Find the greatest number of tickets that the airline can sell for each flight.

question.answer: (a) Ticket-holders turn up independently of one another; the probability of turning up is the same for every ticket-holder. (b) e.g. groups (families, tour groups) travel together, so turning up is not independent. (c) $0.722$ (d) $185$
skills: explaining in context why the independence (or constant-probability) assumption of a binomial model may fail for people who travel together
greatest number of trials $n$ for which a binomial cumulative probability $\mathrm{P}(X \le 180)$ stays at least $0.95$, found by tabulating $n$ on the calculator against a fixed seat count
a binomial built on a binomial: P(X ≥ 181) for X ~ B(184, 0.95) becomes the p of Y ~ B(7, p) over the week
question.solution:
(a) Whether one ticket-holder turns up for the flight is independent of whether any other ticket-holder turns up. The probability that a ticket-holder turns up for the flight is the same (0.95) for every ticket-holder. [B1 each, in context]
(b) Many people buy their tickets together and travel as a group, for example a family or a tour group. If one member of such a group does not turn up (illness, a late taxi), the others are also likely not to turn up, so whether ticket-holders turn up is not independent. [B1] Also accept: the probability of turning up is not the same for every ticket-holder, e.g. business travellers with flexible tickets are more likely to switch flights than holidaymakers with non-refundable tickets.
(c) $X \sim \mathrm{B}(184, 0.95)$. At least one ticket-holder cannot be given a seat means $X \ge 181$; exactly one cannot be given a seat means $X = 181$.
$\mathrm{P}(X \ge 181) = 1 - \mathrm{P}(X \le 180) = 1 - 0.983575 = 0.016425$
$\mathrm{P}(X = 181) = 0.011860$
$\mathrm{P}(X = 181 \mid X \ge 181) = \frac{\mathrm{P}(X = 181)}{\mathrm{P}(X \ge 181)} = \frac{0.011860}{0.016425} = 0.722$ (3 s.f.) [M1 ratio of the two binomial probabilities, A1]
(d) Let $n$ be the number of tickets sold for a flight, so that $X \sim \mathrm{B}(n, 0.95)$. [B1] Every ticket-holder who turns up can be given a seat means $X \le 180$, so we need $\mathrm{P}(X \le 180) \ge 0.95$.
From the graphing calculator: when $n = 184$, $\mathrm{P}(X \le 180) = 0.9836$; when $n = 185$, $\mathrm{P}(X \le 180) = 0.9567 \ge 0.95$; when $n = 186$, $\mathrm{P}(X \le 180) = 0.9071 < 0.95$. [M1 values for $n = 185$ and $n = 186$]
$\mathrm{P}(X \le 180)$ decreases as $n$ increases, so the greatest number of tickets the airline can sell is $185$. [A1]

(c) [revised at moderation] For one flight, X ~ B(184, 0.95): P(X ≥ 181) = 1 − P(X ≤ 180) = 0.01640 (calculator). Let Y be the number of the 7 flights on which someone cannot be seated: Y ~ B(7, 0.0164). P(Y ≥ 2) = 1 − P(Y ≤ 1) = 0.00536. M1 for P(X ≥ 181) = 0.0164, M1 for stating Y ~ B(7, 0.0164), A1 for 0.00536. (d) now [2]: M1 for the two tabulated values P(X ≤ 180) = 0.9567 at n = 185 and 0.9071 at n = 186 (B(n, 0.95) implicit in the tabulation), A1 for 185.
question.syllabus_check: 9758 Section B only: the binomial distribution as a model with its two conditions stated and critiqued in context, binomial probabilities and cumulative probabilities from the graphing calculator, conditional probability $\mathrm{P}(A \mid B) = \mathrm{P}(A \cap B)/\mathrm{P}(B)$ between two binomial events (here $A \subset B$), and an unknown number of trials $n$ fixed by a probability condition by tabulation. No Poisson, no normal approximation to the binomial, no geometric distribution, no cumulative distribution function.
question.originality_note: No earlier Set has a binomial question, and no GCE 9758/9740 paper in the corpus uses an overbooked flight. The real binomial questions of 2019, 2023, 2024 and 2025 (quality-control counts of faulty items: assumptions stated, one probability, a binomial of a binomial over a week, a total over several days) and the 2025 specimen (the range of $p$ from a modal value) all fix $n$ and vary the event or $p$; here the seat count fixes the event and the candidate must introduce the number of trials $n$ as the unknown, the assumption is critiqued rather than only stated, and a conditional probability links two binomial events read from the context. There is no binomial-of-a-binomial, no total over days and no mean-variance relation.

answers.(a): Each ticket-holder turns up (or not) independently of every other ticket-holder; the probability that a ticket-holder turns up is the same, 0.95, for every ticket-holder (on every flight).
answers.(b): Independence may fail: people often buy tickets and travel in groups (families, colleagues), so if one does not turn up the others in the group are also likely not to turn up. (Alternatively, the no-show probability may vary between passengers, e.g. business vs leisure travellers.)
answers.(c): X ~ B(184, 0.95); P(X >= 181) = 0.016425 per flight. Y = number of the 7 flights on which someone cannot be seated, Y ~ B(7, 0.016425); P(Y >= 2) = 1 - P(Y=0) - P(Y=1) = 0.00536 (3 s.f.)
answers.(d): Need P(X <= 180) >= 0.95 with X ~ B(n, 0.95): n = 185 gives 0.9567 >= 0.95, n = 186 gives 0.9071 < 0.95; greatest number of tickets = 185

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both give independence between ticket-holders and a constant probability (0.95) of turning up, each stated in the flight context.

parts.label: (b)
parts.note: Both give the group-travel reason (families, tour groups, colleagues) for independence failing; the setter also accepts the unequal-probability reason (business vs holiday travellers).

parts.label: (d)
parts.note: Both 185. Re-worked: with X ~ B(n, 0.95), P(X <= 180) = 0.9836 (n = 184), 0.9567 (n = 185), 0.9071 (n = 186); decreasing in n, so greatest n is 185.

verdict.key_verdict: The blind examiner and the setter agree on every part, and my own working confirms 0.722 in (c) and 185 in (d); the key is right.

[3]' (the candidate must first find P(X >= 181) = 0.0164 and then set up B(7, 0.0164)); the marks then read 2/1/3/3 = 9, or keep 8 by paying (d) 2 marks (M1 the two tabulated values, A1 185, with B(n, 0.95) implicit in the tabulation).
