question.stem:
Over a long period, the mean journey time of buses on a certain route during the morning peak was $36.0$ minutes. A new system of traffic lights is then installed along the route. A commuters' association believes that the new system has increased the mean morning journey time. The bus company, whose timetable for the route is based on a mean morning journey time of $36.0$ minutes, wishes to find out whether the mean morning journey time is now different from this value. The journey times, $x$ minutes, of a random sample of $50$ morning journeys made after the installation are summarised as follows.
$n = 50, \qquad \sum (x - 35) = 95, \qquad \sum (x - 35)^2 = 768.5$
The association and the bus company each use this sample to carry out a hypothesis test.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Calculate unbiased estimates of the population mean and variance of the morning journey time after the installation.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: State hypotheses for the association's test and for the bus company's test, defining any parameter you use.
parts.answer: $\mu$ minutes = population mean morning journey time after the installation. Association: $\mathrm{H}_0: \mu = 36.0$, $\mathrm{H}_1: \mu > 36.0$. Bus company: $\mathrm{H}_0: \mu = 36.0$, $\mathrm{H}_1: \mu \neq 36.0$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Find the $p$-value of the association's test, and state what this $p$-value means in the context of the question.
parts.answer: $p$-value $= 0.0331$. If the population mean morning journey time is still $36.0$ minutes, the probability that a random sample of $50$ morning journeys has a mean journey time of $36.9$ minutes or more is $0.0331$.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Both tests are carried out at the $\alpha\%$ level of significance. Find the set of values of $\alpha$ for which the association concludes that the mean morning journey time has increased but the bus company does not conclude that the mean morning journey time has changed.

question.answer: (a) $36.9$ minutes, $12$ minutes$^2$; (b) $\mu$ = population mean morning journey time after the installation; association $\mathrm{H}_0: \mu = 36.0$, $\mathrm{H}_1: \mu > 36.0$; bus company $\mathrm{H}_0: \mu = 36.0$, $\mathrm{H}_1: \mu \neq 36.0$; (c) $0.0331$, the probability, if the mean is still $36.0$ minutes, that a random sample of $50$ journeys has mean at least $36.9$ minutes; (d) $3.31 < \alpha < 6.62$
skills: one-tailed and two-tailed hypotheses written for two parties who test the SAME sample with different aims
the p-value of a large-sample z-test (unbiased estimates from data coded about a value other than the hypothesised mean, Central Limit Theorem) and its meaning in context
the band of significance levels at which a one-tailed test rejects H0 but the two-tailed test on the same data does not, from the two-tailed p-value being double the one-tailed one
question.solution:
(a) $\bar{x} = 35 + \frac{95}{50} = 36.9$.
$s^2 = \frac{1}{49}\left[768.5 - \frac{95^2}{50}\right] = \frac{1}{49}(768.5 - 180.5) = \frac{588}{49} = 12$.
Unbiased estimate of the population mean $= 36.9$ minutes; unbiased estimate of the population variance $= 12$ minutes$^2$. [B1 B1] (The data are coded about 35, not about the hypothesised 36.0: $\bar{x} = 35 + 1.9$.)
(b) Let $\mu$ minutes be the population mean morning journey time after the installation.
The association believes the mean has increased, so its test is one-tailed: $\mathrm{H}_0: \mu = 36.0$ against $\mathrm{H}_1: \mu > 36.0$.
The bus company wants to know whether the mean differs from 36.0 in either direction (its timetable is wrong if journeys are longer or shorter), so its test is two-tailed: $\mathrm{H}_0: \mu = 36.0$ against $\mathrm{H}_1: \mu \neq 36.0$. [B1 for $\mu$ defined with the association's pair; B1 for the bus company's pair]
(c) Under $\mathrm{H}_0$, since $n = 50$ is large, by the Central Limit Theorem $\bar{X} \sim \mathrm{N}\left(36.0, \frac{12}{50}\right)$ approximately.
Test statistic $z = \frac{36.9 - 36.0}{\sqrt{12/50}} = \frac{0.9}{\sqrt{0.24}} = 1.837$ (4 s.f.).
$p$-value $= \mathrm{P}(\bar{X} \ge 36.9) = \mathrm{P}(Z \ge 1.8371) = 0.033096 = 0.0331$ (3 s.f.). [B1]
Meaning: assuming the population mean morning journey time is still $36.0$ minutes, the probability that a random sample of $50$ morning journeys has a mean journey time of $36.9$ minutes or more is $0.0331$. [B1]
(d) The bus company's test is two-tailed, so its $p$-value is $\mathrm{P}(|Z| \ge 1.8371) = 2 \times 0.033096 = 0.066193 = 0.0662$ (3 s.f.). [M1]
$\mathrm{H}_0$ is rejected when the $p$-value $\le \frac{\alpha}{100}$.
The association rejects $\mathrm{H}_0$ (concludes that the mean has increased) when $\frac{\alpha}{100} \ge 0.033096$, i.e. $\alpha \ge 3.3096$.
The bus company does not reject $\mathrm{H}_0$ (does not conclude that the mean has changed) when $\frac{\alpha}{100} < 0.066193$, i.e. $\alpha < 6.6193$.
Hence $3.31 < \alpha < 6.62$ (3 s.f.; the end-points are $3.3096\ldots$ and $6.6193\ldots$, so either inequality sign at the left end is accepted). [A1]
[Equivalently, with critical values: the association rejects when $1.837$ exceeds the upper $\frac{\alpha}{100}$ point of $\mathrm{N}(0, 1)$, and the bus company does not reject when $1.837$ is below the upper $\frac{\alpha}{200}$ point.] Note that $\alpha = 5$ lies in this band: at the usual 5% level the two organisations reach different conclusions from the same journeys.
question.syllabus_check: 9758 Section B only: a test of a population mean from a large sample with the variance estimated (z-test via the Central Limit Theorem); unbiased estimates of the population mean and variance from summarised data in the form $\sum (x - a)$, $\sum (x - a)^2$; null and alternative hypotheses with the parameter defined; one-tail and two-tail tests chosen from the aim; the $p$-value and its meaning; the level of significance and the rejection rule. No t-test, no Type I/II error terms, no test of a difference of two means, no Poisson.
question.originality_note: New situation: bus journey times after a traffic-light change, tested on ONE sample by two parties with different aims. The reversed part is new in direction: past papers ask for the least integer $\alpha$ (GCE 2024 P2 Q8), a range of $\alpha$ for one test (GCE 2016 P2 Q6), a range of the variance (GCE 2018 P2 Q5, 2025 specimen P2 Q10) or of $\bar{x}$ (GCE 2011, 2012, 2014); here the candidate must see that the two-tailed $p$-value is double the one-tailed one and find the band of $\alpha$ where the two conclusions disagree. The 2025 specimen has a 2-tail Production Manager and a 1-tail Finance Manager, but with separate samples and no comparison of conclusions; this question compares the two conclusions on the same data and asks for the meaning of the $p$-value in context instead of a Central Limit Theorem explanation. Data coded about 35, not the hypothesised 36.0 (avoids GCE 2010 P2 Q6's 42.0-minute mean and GCE 2011's 38.0). No earlier Set has a hypothesis-testing question.

answers.(a): Unbiased estimate of population mean = 36.9 minutes; unbiased estimate of population variance = 12 (min^2)
answers.(b): Let mu be the population mean morning journey time (minutes) after the installation. Association: H0: mu = 36.0 vs H1: mu > 36.0. Bus company: H0: mu = 36.0 vs H1: mu != 36.0.
answers.(c): Under H0, by CLT (n = 50 large) Xbar ~ N(36, 12/50) approx; z = 1.837, p-value = P(Xbar >= 36.9) = 0.0331 (3 s.f.). Meaning: if the mean morning journey time is still 36.0 minutes, the probability of a random sample of 50 journeys having a mean time of 36.9 minutes or more is 0.0331.
answers.(d): Association rejects H0 iff 0.0331 <= alpha/100; bus company does not reject iff two-tailed p = 0.0662 > alpha/100. Set: {alpha : 3.31 <= alpha < 6.62}

issues: (c)/(d): values assume the large-sample z-test with the sample variance 12 used for sigma^2 (the 9758 convention); a t-test would give slightly different p-values (about 0.036 one-tailed).
(d): the inclusive/strict endpoints follow the convention 'reject H0 when p-value <= significance level'.

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both give mean 36.9 minutes and variance 12 minutes^2. Re-worked: xbar = 35 + 95/50 = 36.9; s^2 = (768.5 - 95^2/50)/49 = 588/49 = 12 exactly. Examination-clean, and the coding about 35 (not the hypothesised 36.0) is a live trap a reflex 36 + 1.9 = 37.9 falls into.

parts.label: (b)
parts.note: Both define mu as the population mean morning journey time after the installation and give H0: mu = 36.0 with H1: mu > 36.0 (association) and H1: mu != 36.0 (bus company). The tails are decisions the candidate makes from 'increased' and 'different from this value' (the timetable sentence justifies the two-tailed choice); the stem states neither tail nor hypotheses.

parts.label: (c)
parts.note: Both: by the CLT (n = 50) Xbar ~ N(36.0, 12/50), z = 0.9/sqrt(0.24) = 1.8371, p = P(Z >= 1.8371) = 0.033096 = 0.0331 (3 s.f.), with the same in-context meaning. Re-worked and confirmed. The blind examiner's remark that a t-test would give about 0.036 is not a disagreement: 9758 uses the large-sample z-test with s^2 for sigma^2, and the t-test is outside the syllabus.

parts.label: (d)
parts.note: Two-tailed p-value 2 x 0.033096 = 0.066193 = 0.0662; association rejects when alpha/100 >= 0.033096, bus company does not reject when alpha/100 < 0.066193; band 3.31 <= alpha < 6.62. Setter writes 3.31 < alpha < 6.62 and accepts either sign at the left end; blind writes 3.31 <= alpha < 6.62. Same set to 3 s.f., differing only in the endpoint convention (reject when p <= alpha/100), which the setter already allows. alpha is real here (2024 P2 Q8 said integer), so an interval is the right form; the 5% level sits inside it, which is the point of the question.

verdict.key_verdict: The setter and the blind examiner agree on every part; I re-worked all four (xbar = 36.9, s^2 = 12 exactly, z = 1.837, one-tailed p = 0.03310, two-tailed 0.06619, band 3.31 <= alpha < 6.62) and the key is right, the only difference being the inclusive sign at the left end of (d), a convention the setter accepts either way.
fixes: Add the one-mark in-context reason about the sample or the distribution that every 2022-2024 hypothesis-test question carries and this one lacks (2022 P2 Q11(e) two assumptions, 2023 P2 Q8(a)(ii) why the sample is unsuitable, 2024 P2 Q8(e) whether 10 mornings suffice): e.g. '(e) Explain why the association was able to carry out its test without knowing the distribution of the journey times. [1]' (the Central Limit Theorem in words, n = 50 large), or '(e) The bus company later repeats its test with a random sample of 8 morning journeys. State an assumption it must now make. [1]'. This takes the slot to 9 marks; if the session must hold 8, fold it into (c) as 'Find the p-value of the association's test, explaining why the distribution of journey times need not be known, and state what this p-value means in the context of the question. [3]' and let the session take one mark from a routine part elsewhere. Marks otherwise match 2022-2024 pay within one mark (estimates [2], hypotheses defined [2], p-value + meaning [2], the two-tailed p-value and the band [2]), so no re-mark is needed.
verdict.why: A genuine 2024-shape hypothesis question: the two parties make the tail a decision inside (b) rather than a printed one, the coding about 35 rather than the hypothesised 36.0 is a real twist in (a), and (d) turns the 2024 P2 Q8(c) idea (a p-value read as a significance level) into a band between the one- and two-tailed p-values on the same data - one idea supplied by the candidate, clean numbers (s^2 = 12), SEAB register, finishable in the 14 minutes 8 marks buy, and no Set 1 P1 or in-paper skill anywhere near it (nearest Jaccard 0.068 to GCE 2024 P2 Q8, 0.013 to Set 1 P1 Q6; gates passed). It is one light edit short of indistinguishable: every real 2022-2024 hypothesis question also asks a one-mark reason about the sample or the distribution, and this asks none.

question.stem:
An ecologist visits 8 islands in an archipelago. For each island she records its area, $A$ km$^{2}$, and the number, $S$, of species of resident bird found on the island. The results are shown in the table.

$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline A & 0.3 & 0.8 & 1.5 & 2.6 & 4.2 & 7.0 & 11.5 & 18.4 \\ \hline S & 20 & 28 & 34 & 38 & 44 & 52 & 60 & 72 \\ \hline \end{array}$

A scatter diagram for the data is shown below.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: The scatter diagram shows the data. Explain what the scatter diagram tells you about the way in which $S$ changes as $A$ increases.
parts.answer: As $A$ increases, $S$ increases, but by less and less for each extra km$^2$: the points rise steeply at first and then flatten, so the relationship is not linear.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: The ecologist considers the two models $S = a + b\ln A$ and $S = kA^{n}$, where $a$, $b$, $k$ and $n$ are constants. By calculating a suitable product moment correlation coefficient for each model, determine which model gives the better fit to the data, and find the values of the constants for that model. Give each product moment correlation coefficient correct to 4 decimal places.
parts.answer: $r$ between $\ln A$ and $S$ is $0.9772$; $r$ between $\ln A$ and $\ln S$ is $0.9984$, which is closer to 1, so $S = kA^{n}$ is the better model. $\ln S = 3.37 + 0.301\ln A$, so $n = 0.301$ and $k = 29.2$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: In this part you should use the model you chose in part (b).

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.text: Two islands $P$ and $Q$ in the archipelago are such that $P$ has twice as many species of resident bird as $Q$. Find the ratio of the area of $P$ to the area of $Q$.

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.text: An island in the archipelago that the ecologist did not visit has area $6.0$ km$^{2}$. Estimate the number of species of resident bird on this island, and explain whether your estimate is reliable.
subparts.answer: About 50 species ($S = 50.0$). Reliable: $A = 6.0$ lies within the range of the data, $0.3 \leqslant A \leqslant 18.4$, and $r = 0.9984$ is very close to 1.

skills: linearising a power model $S = kA^{n}$ by regressing $\ln S$ on $\ln A$ (both variables transformed) and recovering $k = \mathrm{e}^{c}$ from the intercept
choosing between a logarithmic model $S = a + b\ln A$ and a power model by comparing the product moment correlation coefficients of their linearised forms
using the power law to find the area ratio for a doubled count, $(A_P/A_Q)^{n} = 2$ with $k$ cancelling, then an interpolated estimate judged for reliability
question.figure_description: A scatter diagram of the 8 data points only, no line and no curve. Horizontal axis A (km²) from 0 to 20 with ticks every 5; vertical axis S (number of species) from 0 to 80 with ticks every 20; axes labelled A and S with O at the origin; a light grid is acceptable. Plot exactly these points as small crosses or dots: (0.3, 20), (0.8, 28), (1.5, 34), (2.6, 38), (4.2, 44), (7.0, 52), (11.5, 60), (18.4, 72). Nothing else is printed: no regression line, no equation, no labels on the points.
question.solution:
(a) Sketch: $A$ on the horizontal axis (0 to 20), $S$ on the vertical axis (0 to 80), 8 points plotted. For small $A$ the points rise steeply ($S$ goes from 20 to 38 as $A$ goes from 0.3 to 2.6); for larger $A$ they rise more slowly ($S$ goes from 44 to 72 as $A$ goes from 4.2 to 18.4). The points lie close to a curve that is concave downwards.
As $A$ increases, $S$ increases, but at a decreasing rate, so a linear model $S = c + dA$ is not appropriate (even though $r$ between $A$ and $S$ is $0.957$). [B1 sketch, B1 description]

(b) Model $S = a + b\ln A$ is linear in $\ln A$ and $S$: $r$ between $\ln A$ and $S$ $= 0.97721\ldots = 0.9772$ (4 d.p.). [B1]
Model $S = kA^{n}$: taking logarithms, $\ln S = \ln k + n\ln A$, which is linear in $\ln A$ and $\ln S$: $r$ between $\ln A$ and $\ln S$ $= 0.99843\ldots = 0.9984$ (4 d.p.). [B1]
Since $0.9984$ is closer to 1 than $0.9772$, the model $S = kA^{n}$ gives the better fit. [B1]
Least squares regression line of $\ln S$ on $\ln A$ (from the calculator): $\ln S = 3.3737 + 0.30087\ln A$.
So $n = 0.301$ (3 s.f.) and $\ln k = 3.3737$, giving $k = \mathrm{e}^{3.3737} = 29.19 = 29.2$ (3 s.f.). [B1 both]
(Using $\lg$ instead: $\lg S = 1.4652 + 0.30087\lg A$, the same $r$ and $n$, and $k = 10^{1.4652} = 29.2$.)
(For comparison, the other model's line is $S = 30.4 + 12.1\ln A$, which would even give $S < 0$ for $A < 0.081$, unrealistic for a very small island.)

(c)(i) Let the areas be $A_P$ and $A_Q$. Then $kA_P^{\,n} = 2kA_Q^{\,n}$, so $\left(\frac{A_P}{A_Q}\right)^{n} = 2$ ($k$ cancels, so the ratio is the same for any such pair of islands). [M1]
$\frac{A_P}{A_Q} = 2^{\frac{1}{n}} = 2^{\frac{1}{0.30087}} = 10.01\ldots = 10.0$ (3 s.f.) (with $n = 0.301$: $2^{\frac{1}{0.301}} = 10.0$). [A1]
So an island with twice as many species of resident bird has about 10 times the area.

(c)(ii) $S = 29.19 \times 6.0^{0.30087}$: $\ln S = 3.3737 + 0.30087\ln 6 = 3.9128$, so $S = 50.04 \approx 50$ species (with $k = 29.2$, $n = 0.301$: $S = 50.1 \approx 50$). [B1]
The estimate is reliable: $A = 6.0$ lies within the range of the data ($0.3 \leqslant A \leqslant 18.4$), so this is interpolation, and $r = 0.9984$ is very close to 1, so $\ln S$ and $\ln A$ have a strong linear relationship. [B1]
question.syllabus_check: 9758 Correlation and linear regression: a scatter diagram and what it shows; the product moment correlation coefficient as a measure of linear fit and the choice between candidate models by comparing r; a logarithmic transformation to achieve linearity (the syllabus's 'square, reciprocal, logarithmic or other transformation'); the least squares regression line of y on x from the graphing calculator (ln S on ln A, the area being the independent variable); interpolation and the reliability of an estimate. Reducing y = kx^n to ln y = ln k + n ln x is O-Level A Math linear law (assumed knowledge). No formulae derived, no hypothesis test on r, no r^2 = b1b2. Section B only; calculator values read (r to 4 d.p. as stated, constants to 3 s.f.).
question.originality_note: No SEAB regression question (2008-2025 and the 2025 specimen) or earlier Set uses a species-area situation, and no earlier Set has a regression question at all. Every SEAB model comparison transforms ONE variable (x^2, x^3, ln x, sqrt x, 1/x, e^y, ln y); this one needs a power model with an unknown exponent, linearised in BOTH variables (ln S on ln A) with k recovered from the intercept. GCE 2024 P2 Q11(a) compares ln m with sqrt m for cereal prices and ends in a price estimate; here the log model's rival is a free-exponent power law, and part (c)(i), the area ratio for twice as many species where k cancels and the answer holds for any pair of islands, has no counterpart in any real paper. The sequence scatter -> two models -> property of the model -> estimate is not that of GCE 2023 P2 Q7, 2025 P2 Q8 or the 2025 specimen (pumpkin masses, d^2 against d^3).

answers.(a): Scatter diagram of S against A: points rise steeply for small A then level off (concave curve). S increases as A increases, but at a decreasing rate (non-linear).
answers.(b): S = a + b ln A: r (between ln A and S) = 0.9772; S = kA^n: r (between ln A and ln S) = 0.9984. |r| is closer to 1 for S = kA^n, so S = kA^n is the better model. ln S = 3.3737 + 0.30087 ln A, giving k = 29.2, n = 0.301 (S = 29.2A^0.301).
answers.(c)(i): A_P/A_Q = 2^(1/n) = 2^(1/0.301) = 10.0 (area of P is about 10 times area of Q)
answers.(c)(ii): S = 29.2(6.0)^0.301 = 50.0, i.e. about 50 species. Reliable: A = 6.0 lies within the data range 0.3 to 18.4 (interpolation) and r = 0.9984 is very close to 1, so the model fits the data very well.

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both describe the same picture: points rising steeply for small A then more gradually (concave), S increasing at a decreasing rate, not linear. Slopes between consecutive points fall from 16 to 1.7, so the curvature is real on a sketch.

parts.label: (b)
parts.note: Recomputed: r(ln A, S) = 0.97721 -> 0.9772; r(ln A, ln S) = 0.99843 -> 0.9984; ln S = 3.3737 + 0.30087 ln A, so n = 0.301 and k = e^3.3737 = 29.2. Setter and examiner identical; S = kA^n is the better model.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.note: (A_P/A_Q)^n = 2 with k cancelling; 2^(1/0.30087) = 10.012 and 2^(1/0.301) = 10.002, both 10.0 to 3 s.f. Setter and examiner identical.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.note: 29.19 x 6.0^0.30087 = 50.04, or 29.2 x 6.0^0.301 = 50.07: about 50 species. Reliable, A = 6.0 inside 0.3..18.4 and r = 0.9984. Setter and examiner identical.

verdict.key_verdict: No disagreement anywhere: every value in the setter's key is confirmed by the blind examiner and by an independent recomputation of the two correlation coefficients, the regression line, the area ratio and the estimate.
fixes: Print the scatter diagram in the question, as GCE 2022 P2 Q10 and GCE 2024 P2 Q11 do (no 2022-2024 regression question had the candidate draw one, and this data is log-spread: A = 0.3, 0.8 and 1.5 fall within the first 8% of a 0-20 axis). Then re-mark: (a) becomes 'Explain what the scatter diagram tells you about the way in which S changes as A increases' [1], and (b) gains the mark [5], matching GCE 2023 P2 Q7's 1 + 1 for the two coefficients and 3 for the choice with the constants; the total stays 10.
verdict.why: The species-area power law is a real context whose data give n = 0.30 (the ecological value), the transformation is left to the candidate and needs both variables logged, which no 2022-2024 paper asked, (c)(i) is a genuine use of the model with k cancelling, and the three explain units and the marks sit exactly where GCE 2023 P2 Q7 and GCE 2024 P2 Q11(a) put them. The shared scatter -> two models by r -> line -> estimate skeleton is the roster's fixed shape for this slot, not a re-skin; the one thing a 2022-2024 paper would do differently is print the scatter diagram for data spread like this rather than have it sketched.

question.stem:
In a penalty kick, the kicker kicks the ball towards either the left side or the right side of the goal and, at the same moment, the goalkeeper dives towards either the left side or the right side of the goal. When the goalkeeper dives towards the side to which the ball is kicked, the probability that a goal is scored is $0.3$. When the goalkeeper dives towards the other side, the probability that a goal is scored is $0.9$.
Kofi takes penalty kicks against the goalkeeper Lim. On each kick, Kofi kicks towards the left side with probability $0.6$ and Lim dives towards the left side with probability $p$, where $0 \le p \le 1$. Kofi's choice and Lim's choice are independent of each other.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Show that the probability that Kofi scores a goal with a penalty kick is $0.66 - 0.12p$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Kofi wonders whether the side he kicks towards affects his chance of scoring.
parts.answer: (i) $p = 0.5$; (ii) Kofi's chance of scoring is the same whichever side he kicks towards.

subparts.label: (i)
subparts.text: Find the value of $p$ for which the events 'Kofi kicks towards the left side' and 'Kofi scores a goal' are independent.

subparts.label: (ii)
subparts.text: Explain, in the context of the question, what this independence means for Kofi.
subparts.answer: When $p = 0.5$, Kofi scores with probability $0.6$ whichever side he kicks towards, so he cannot increase his chance of scoring by changing the side he kicks towards (or how often he chooses the left side).

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: For the value of $p$ found in part (b)(i), find the probability that, given that Kofi does not score a goal with a particular penalty kick, Lim dived towards the side to which the ball was kicked.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text:
Kofi and Lim now play a game in which Kofi takes a sequence of penalty kicks against Lim. A kick that does not result in a goal is called a miss. Kofi wins the game as soon as the total number of goals he has scored in the game is 2 more than the total number of misses, and Lim wins the game as soon as the total number of misses is 2 more than the total number of goals. The probability that Kofi scores a goal with any one kick is $g$, where $0 < g < 1$, and the outcomes of different kicks are independent.
Show that the probability that Kofi wins the game is $\frac{g^2}{1 - 2g + 2g^2}$.

parts.label: (e)
parts.text: Throughout the game, Kofi and Lim make their choices on every kick with the probabilities given at the start of the question, using the same value of $p$ on every kick. Lim wants the probability that Kofi wins the game to be less than $0.6$. Find the range of values of $p$ that Lim could choose.

question.answer: (a) $0.66 - 0.12p$ (shown). (b)(i) $p = 0.5$. (b)(ii) Kofi scores with probability $0.6$ whichever side he kicks towards, so changing his side cannot improve his chance of scoring. (c) $0.875$. (d) $\frac{g^2}{1 - 2g + 2g^2}$ (shown). (e) $0.912 < p \le 1$.
skills: independence of two events used as an equation to find an unknown probability from a tree, then interpreted in context
a 'win by two clear' repeated-trial game: kicks taken in pairs from level, winning probability summed as a geometric series
a probability inequality solved as a quadratic in g (root above 1 rejected) and carried back through g = 0.66 - 0.12p to a range of the underlying parameter
question.solution:
Let $L$ = Kofi kicks towards the left side, $K$ = Lim dives towards the left side, $G$ = a goal is scored. $\mathrm{P}(L) = 0.6$, $\mathrm{P}(K) = p$, $L$ and $K$ independent.

(a) Tree: first branch $L$ / $L'$, second branch $K$ / $K'$, third branch $G$ / $G'$ (0.3 when the dive matches the kick, 0.9 otherwise).
$\mathrm{P}(G) = 0.6[0.3p + 0.9(1 - p)] + 0.4[0.9p + 0.3(1 - p)]$ [M1: all four branches]
$= 0.6(0.9 - 0.6p) + 0.4(0.3 + 0.6p) = 0.54 - 0.36p + 0.12 + 0.24p = 0.66 - 0.12p$ (shown) [A1]

(b)(i) $\mathrm{P}(L \cap G) = 0.6[0.3p + 0.9(1 - p)] = 0.6(0.9 - 0.6p) = 0.54 - 0.36p$.
$\mathrm{P}(L)\,\mathrm{P}(G) = 0.6(0.66 - 0.12p) = 0.396 - 0.072p$.
Independent $\iff 0.54 - 0.36p = 0.396 - 0.072p$ [M1] $\iff 0.144 = 0.288p \iff p = 0.5$ [A1].
(Equivalently $\mathrm{P}(G \mid L) = \mathrm{P}(G)$: $0.9 - 0.6p = 0.66 - 0.12p$.)

(b)(ii) With $p = 0.5$: $\mathrm{P}(G \mid L) = 0.3p + 0.9(1 - p) = 0.15 + 0.45 = 0.6$ and $\mathrm{P}(G \mid L') = 0.9p + 0.3(1 - p) = 0.45 + 0.15 = 0.6$. Kofi's probability of scoring is $0.6$ whichever side he kicks towards, so he cannot increase his chance of scoring against Lim by changing the side he kicks towards. [B1]

(c) $p = 0.5$. Let $S$ = Lim dives towards the side to which the ball is kicked.
$\mathrm{P}(S) = \mathrm{P}(L)\mathrm{P}(K) + \mathrm{P}(L')\mathrm{P}(K') = 0.6(0.5) + 0.4(0.5) = 0.5$, so $\mathrm{P}(S \cap G') = 0.5 \times 0.7 = 0.35$ [M1: both matching branches].
$\mathrm{P}(G') = 1 - (0.66 - 0.06) = 0.4$.
$\mathrm{P}(S \mid G') = \frac{0.35}{0.4} = 0.875$ [A1].

(d) Let $d$ = (goals so far) $-$ (misses so far). The game starts with $d = 0$, each kick changes $d$ by $+1$ (probability $g$) or $-1$ (probability $1 - g$), and the game ends when $d = 2$ (Kofi wins) or $d = -2$ (Lim wins).
From $d = 0$ one kick gives $d = \pm 1$, so the game cannot end after an odd number of kicks. Taking the kicks in pairs from $d = 0$: two goals, probability $g^2$ (Kofi wins); two misses, probability $(1 - g)^2$ (Lim wins); one of each in either order, probability $2g(1 - g)$, and $d = 0$ again [M1].
So Kofi wins after 2, 4, 6, ... kicks with probabilities $g^2$, $2g(1 - g)g^2$, $[2g(1 - g)]^2 g^2$, ...
$\mathrm{P}(\text{Kofi wins}) = g^2\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}[2g(1 - g)]^k$ [M1: geometric series, first term $g^2$, common ratio $2g(1 - g)$], convergent since $0 < 2g(1 - g) \le \frac{1}{2} < 1$,
$= \frac{g^2}{1 - 2g(1 - g)} = \frac{g^2}{1 - 2g + 2g^2}$ (shown) [A1].
(Alternative: with $w$ = P(Kofi wins from $d = 0$), $w = g^2 + 2g(1 - g)w$, giving the same result.)

(e) From part (a), $g = 0.66 - 0.12p$, so $0.54 \le g \le 0.66$ [M1: link to part (a)].
Need $\frac{g^2}{1 - 2g + 2g^2} < 0.6$. Since $1 - 2g + 2g^2 = g^2 + (1 - g)^2 > 0$:
$g^2 < 0.6 - 1.2g + 1.2g^2 \iff 0.2g^2 - 1.2g + 0.6 > 0 \iff g^2 - 6g + 3 > 0 \iff g < 3 - \sqrt{6}$ or $g > 3 + \sqrt{6}$.
As $0 < g < 1$, reject $g > 3 + \sqrt{6}$; so $g < 3 - \sqrt{6} \approx 0.5505$ [M1].
$0.66 - 0.12p < 3 - \sqrt{6} \iff p > \frac{\sqrt{6} - 2.34}{0.12} = \frac{50\sqrt{6} - 117}{6} = 0.91241\ldots$
With $p \le 1$: $0.912 < p \le 1$ [A1].
(GC route: graph $y = \frac{(0.66 - 0.12x)^2}{1 - 2(0.66 - 0.12x) + 2(0.66 - 0.12x)^2}$ for $0 \le x \le 1$; it is decreasing and meets $y = 0.6$ at $x = 0.912$.)
Check: $p = 1$ gives $g = 0.54$ and $\frac{0.2916}{0.5032} = 0.579 < 0.6$; $p = 0.9$ gives $g = 0.552$ and probability $0.603 > 0.6$. In context, Lim must dive towards Kofi's favoured (left) side on more than about $91\%$ of kicks.

parts.note: Both give p = 0.5. Checked: P(G | L) = 0.9 - 0.6p = P(G) = 0.66 - 0.12p gives 0.48p = 0.24.

verdict.key_verdict: Setter and blind examiner agree on every part and I confirm each; the key is exactly right, both show-that targets are true, and the range in (e) is non-empty inside 0 <= p <= 1.

question.stem:
In this question you should state the parameters of any distributions you use.
A doctor at a clinic sees her patients one after another, with no gaps between consultations. The duration, in minutes, of a routine consultation follows the distribution $\mathrm{N}(8, 2^2)$. You should assume that the durations of all consultations are independent.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Find the probability that a randomly chosen routine consultation lasts more than 11 minutes.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: The doctor's morning session lasts 2 hours. Find the largest value of $n$ for which the probability that the total duration of $n$ routine consultations is more than 2 hours is less than $0.01$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Explain, in the context of the question, why the assumption that the durations of the consultations in one session are independent may not be valid.
parts.answer: For example: if the doctor falls behind after a long consultation, she may shorten the later consultations to catch up, so the duration of one consultation can affect the durations of the consultations after it.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: The duration, in minutes, of a new-patient consultation follows the distribution $\mathrm{N}(\mu, 3^2)$. The probability that a randomly chosen new-patient consultation lasts more than twice as long as a randomly chosen routine consultation is $0.8$. Find $\mu$.

parts.label: (e)
parts.text: Without doing any detailed calculation, explain whether the probability that a randomly chosen new-patient consultation lasts longer than the total duration of two randomly chosen routine consultations is greater than $0.8$ or less than $0.8$.
parts.answer: Greater than $0.8$: $N - (R_1 + R_2) \sim \mathrm{N}(\mu - 16, 17)$ has the same mean $\mu - 16$ as $N - 2R \sim \mathrm{N}(\mu - 16, 25)$, and this mean is positive (since $0.8 > 0.5$), but its variance is smaller ($17 < 25$), so a greater proportion of its distribution lies above 0.

parts.label: (f)
parts.text: On a certain morning the doctor sees her first patient at 9 a.m., and she has 4 new-patient consultations and 5 routine consultations booked. Find, in whole minutes after 9 a.m., the earliest time at which the probability that she has finished all 9 consultations is at least $0.95$.

question.answer: (a) $0.0668$; (b) $n = 12$; (c) the doctor may shorten later consultations when running late, so durations in a session may depend on each other; (d) $\mu = 20.2$; (e) greater than $0.8$ (same positive mean $\mu - 16$, smaller variance $17 < 25$); (f) 11.14 a.m.
skills: largest integer n for which the total of n independent normal durations exceeds a fixed 2-hour session with probability below 0.01: variance 4n (a sum, not nR) with n in both mean and variance, found from a calculator table

unknown mean found from P(N > 2R) = 0.8, where 'twice as long' is the multiple 2R with variance 4Var(R), reversed through the inverse normal; then 2R against R_1 + R_2 compared by variance alone (same positive mean) to judge a probability without calculating it
earliest whole-minute time for which a mixed total of 4 + 5 independent normal durations is complete with probability at least 0.95: inverse normal rounded UP, not to the nearest minute
question.solution:
Let $R$ minutes be the duration of a routine consultation, $R \sim \mathrm{N}(8, 2^2)$, and $N$ minutes that of a new-patient consultation.
(a) $\mathrm{P}(R > 11) = 0.066807 = 0.0668$ (3 s.f.). [B1]
(b) Let $T_n = R_1 + R_2 + \cdots + R_n$, the total duration of $n$ independent routine consultations. $\mathrm{E}(T_n) = 8n$ and $\mathrm{Var}(T_n) = n \times 2^2 = 4n$ (a sum of $n$ independent durations, not $nR$, whose variance would be $4n^2$), so $T_n \sim \mathrm{N}(8n, 4n)$. [B1]
Require $\mathrm{P}(T_n > 120) < 0.01$. From a table of values on the calculator: [M1]
$n = 12$: $T_{12} \sim \mathrm{N}(96, 48)$, $\mathrm{P}(T_{12} > 120) = 0.000266 < 0.01$;
$n = 13$: $T_{13} \sim \mathrm{N}(104, 52)$, $\mathrm{P}(T_{13} > 120) = 0.0133 > 0.01$;
$n = 14$: $\mathrm{P}(T_{14} > 120) = 0.143$, and the probability increases with $n$.
So the largest $n$ is $n = 12$. [A1]
(Common errors: using the mean alone gives $n = 14$ or $15$; using $\mathrm{Var} = 4n^2$ gives $n = 9$.)
(c) The durations may depend on each other: for example, if the doctor falls behind schedule after a long consultation, she may hurry the later consultations to catch up, so a long consultation tends to be followed by shorter ones. (Also acceptable: a doctor who is ahead of time may spend longer with later patients.) [B1]
(d) $N \sim \mathrm{N}(\mu, 3^2)$. 'More than twice as long' is $N > 2R$, a multiple of ONE routine consultation. $\mathrm{E}(N - 2R) = \mu - 2(8) = \mu - 16$ [B1] and $\mathrm{Var}(N - 2R) = 3^2 + 2^2 \times 2^2 = 9 + 16 = 25$ [B1], so $N - 2R \sim \mathrm{N}(\mu - 16, 25)$.
$\mathrm{P}(N - 2R > 0) = 0.8 \Rightarrow \mathrm{P}\left(Z > \frac{0 - (\mu - 16)}{5}\right) = 0.8 \Rightarrow \frac{16 - \mu}{5} = -0.841621$ [M1]
$\mu = 16 + 5(0.841621) = 20.208 = 20.2$ (3 s.f.). [A1]
(Using $R_1 + R_2$ in place of $2R$, variance $17$, gives the wrong value $19.5$.)
(e) $N - (R_1 + R_2) \sim \mathrm{N}(\mu - 16, 3^2 + 2^2 + 2^2) = \mathrm{N}(\mu - 16, 17)$, which has the same mean as $N - 2R \sim \mathrm{N}(\mu - 16, 25)$ but a smaller variance, $17 < 25$. [B1]
The common mean $\mu - 16 \approx 4.21$ is positive (because $\mathrm{P}(N - 2R > 0) = 0.8 > 0.5$), so the less spread-out distribution has a greater proportion of its area above 0. Hence the probability is greater than $0.8$. [B1]
(Check, not required: $\mathrm{P}(N - R_1 - R_2 > 0) = 0.846$.)
(f) Let $T = N_1 + N_2 + N_3 + N_4 + R_1 + \cdots + R_5$. $\mathrm{E}(T) = 4\mu + 5(8) = 4(20.208) + 40 = 120.83$ and $\mathrm{Var}(T) = 4(3^2) + 5(2^2) = 56$, so $T \sim \mathrm{N}(120.83, 56)$. [B1]
She has finished by $t$ minutes after 9 a.m. when $T \le t$. $\mathrm{P}(T \le t) \geqslant 0.95 \Rightarrow t \geqslant 120.83 + 1.64485\sqrt{56} = 133.14$. [M1]
The earliest whole number of minutes is $t = 134$, rounding UP: $\mathrm{P}(T \le 133) = 0.948 < 0.95$ but $\mathrm{P}(T \le 134) = 0.961 \geqslant 0.95$. So the earliest time is 134 minutes after 9 a.m., i.e. 11.14 a.m. [A1]
(With $\mu = 20.2$: $T \sim \mathrm{N}(120.8, 56)$, $t \geqslant 133.11$, the same answer 11.14 a.m.; rounding to the nearest minute, 11.13 a.m., is wrong.)
question.syllabus_check: 9758 Normal distribution only: probabilities and inverse probabilities from the graphing calculator; E and Var of aX + bY for independent normals; the sum of n independent copies X_1 + ... + X_n against the multiple 2X (listed in the syllabus); an unknown mean found from a given probability; an explanation of the independence assumption in context. No normal approximation, no Poisson, no t-test, no covariance (part (e) needs only that two normals with the same positive mean differ in variance).
question.originality_note: A clinic doctor's consultation durations: no 2022-2024 GCE question, and no earlier question in the corpus, uses this situation. It avoids the exemplars' structures: 2023 P2 Q9 (planks: a total of 8, an expected number, 'differs by less than', L/3 > R/2 then a wastage remark), 2024 P2 Q10 (plates: 5% reduction, binomial of a normal, a Value pack exceeded by 5%), 2021 P2 Q10 and 2017 P2 Q10 (mean and sd from two percentages, a component total), 2018 P2 Q10 (bulb, box and padding), 2020 P2 Q6 (a commute and lateness), 2025 P2 Q10 (two machines and a test). Here the unknown is n in both mean and variance (b), the mean is found BACKWARDS from a condition on N - 2R (d), the sum-versus-multiple distinction is asked as reasoning about variance (e), and the inverse normal must be rounded UP to a whole minute (f). No earlier Set has a Distributions (Normal) question (Set 1 Paper 1 is pure mathematics).

answers.(c): Durations in one session may be related: e.g. if the doctor is running late after a long consultation she may hurry (shorten) the later ones, or tiredness later in the session may make later consultations longer, so one duration affects the next
answers.(e): Greater than 0.8. Y - (X1 + X2) ~ N(μ - 16, 17): same mean μ - 16 (> 0, about 4.21) as Y - 2X but smaller variance (17 < 25), so (μ - 16)/√17 > (μ - 16)/5 and P(Y - (X1 + X2) > 0) > 0.8

parts.label: (b)
parts.note: Both n = 12 with T_n ~ N(8n, 4n). Checked: P(T_12 > 120) = 0.000266 < 0.01, P(T_13 > 120) = 0.0133 > 0.01, and the probability rises with n, so 12 is the largest. (Var = 4n^2 would give 9; the mean alone gives 14 or 15.)

parts.label: (c)
parts.note: Both give a dependence-in-context reason (a long consultation makes the doctor hurry the later ones; the examiner adds tiredness lengthening later ones). Either is a valid B1.

parts.label: (d)
parts.note: Both mu = 20.208 = 20.2 (3 s.f.) from N - 2R ~ N(mu - 16, 25). Checked: invNorm(0.2) = -0.84162, mu = 16 + 5(0.84162) = 20.208. Using R_1 + R_2 (variance 17) gives 19.5, wrong.

parts.label: (e)
parts.note: Both 'greater than 0.8': N - (R_1 + R_2) ~ N(mu - 16, 17) has the same positive mean as N - 2R ~ N(mu - 16, 25) and a smaller variance, so more of it lies above 0. Checked: the actual value is 0.846.

parts.label: (f)
parts.note: Both 134 minutes after 9 a.m. = 11.14 a.m. Checked: T ~ N(120.83, 56), t >= 120.83 + 1.6449 sqrt(56) = 133.14; P(T <= 133) = 0.948 < 0.95, P(T <= 134) = 0.961. With mu rounded to 20.2, t >= 133.11, the same 134; rounding to the nearest minute (11.13 a.m.) is wrong.

verdict.key_verdict: No disagreement anywhere: the setter's key and the blind examiner match on every part and every value re-derives (0.0668; n = 12; mu = 20.2; greater than 0.8; 11.14 a.m.).
fixes: Same skill already in this paper: Q6(b) finds the greatest n by tabulating a cumulative probability on the calculator (binomial overbooking); Q10(b) repeats that method for the normal sum. The distinct content of (b) is the variance 4n with n in both parameters, which Q6 does not test, so the session may accept the overlap; otherwise replace (b) with a normal skill not yet in the paper, e.g. the probability that the 12 consultations booked for the morning session take more than 10 minutes longer in total than the 10 booked for the afternoon session [3] (a difference of two independent sums, variance 4(12) + 4(10) = 88, the GCE 2023 P2 Q9(d) skill), keeping 'largest n by table' for Q6 alone.

Light wording edits to SEAB's register: (b) 'Find the largest value of n for which the probability that the total duration of n routine consultations is more than 2 hours is less than 0.01.'; (f) 'Find, in whole minutes after 9 a.m., the earliest time at which the probability that she has finished all 9 consultations is at least 0.95.' (keep 'whole minutes', never 'to the nearest minute', since rounding UP is the point).
verdict.why: A clean 14-mark Section B closer at the 2022-2024 standard: the candidate must decide that 'twice as long as a randomly chosen consultation' is 2R (variance 16) and not R_1 + R_2, argue (e) from the variance alone without calculating, and round UP to a whole minute in (f) because the context says 'at least 0.95' - three reasons in context, every number examination-clean, no part needing two ideas, about 24 minutes of work. Shares only the boilerplate opener and a 1-mark read with GCE 2023 P2 Q9 (Jaccard 0.055) and no situation or part sequence; nothing in this Set's Paper 1 is statistics. Held at 4 because (b) re-uses Q6's 'largest n by calculator table' method inside the same paper and two parts read a shade wordier than SEAB.
